Below the threshold, the run goes ahead and each zone is watered for less, as described next. Zones in a greenhouse sensor group still water. The panel keeps two settings behind the one switch (skip_irrigation_on_precipitation and forecast_rain_credit): the switch shows on when either is on, and turning it on or off sets both.

Below the threshold the duration is reduced in proportion. When a run starts, each zone is watered for the rain forecast to fall in the 24 hours after the start, less: the forecast hours are weighted by the probability the weather service gives, so 10 mm at 30% counts for 3 mm, and a forecast of 4 mm against a 10 mm deficit waters 6 mm. It works alongside the skip above, which stays all or nothing. A greenhouse zone is not reduced, and a forecast that cannot be read leaves the run as calculated.

Like the rain history below, it shortens the run and leaves the deficit in the water balance. The rain that really falls is measured and credited at the next calculation, so nothing is counted twice, and a forecast that does not come true is made up at the next run. The hours are counted from the moment the run starts, not from the calculation, which on a morning run is hours earlier. The forecast hours come from Open-Meteo, including for installations using another weather service. * Rain sensor. Skip while a binary sensor that is on in the rain says it is raining.

On the advanced panel, that same sensor can do more than veto today: shorten runs after recent rain reads its history over the last five days, weighted so that yesterday counts for more than four days ago, and shortens the run by the result. A day of reported rain today takes the whole run, four days ago takes a tenth of it, and a wet week takes everything.

It is for one case and it applies to one case: a zone whose sensor group reports no rain in millimetres at all, neither a gauge's depth nor a service's rate. Where millimetres exist, the water balance already carries them, decides for itself how long rain keeps counting, and this stays out of the way.

It never touches the balance, because it does not know how much fell. The deficit stays where it was and is watered off once the weather turns, which is the safe direction: a run that was shortened too much is made up tomorrow, while water that was never owed cannot be taken back out of the ground. It needs a sensor that stays on while it rains; one that pulses briefly per bucket tip spends almost no time on and will barely register.

The idea of weighting rain over a few rolling days comes from kloggy's HA-Irrigation-Version2 package, which does it with history_stats over five 24-hour windows. * Freeze. Skip when the temperature is at or below the threshold, 2 °C (36 °F) unless you set one. It reads the sensor you choose, or the weather service's current temperature when none is set. * Wind. Skip when the wind is at or above the threshold, 20 km/h (12 mph) unless you set one: in strong wind a sprinkler waters the path rather than the bed. It reads the sensor you choose, or the weather service's current wind. The weather service's wind is stored at 2 m for the evaporation, and is taken back up to the 10 m that forecasts and wind limits are quoted at. * Days between irrigation, on the same page (see Days between irrigation events).

Thresholds are entered in your unit system and a sensor is read in its own unit, so a sensor in °F works on a metric installation.

Soil moisture is set on each zone rather than here; the page lists the zones that have a sensor, with their threshold, each a link to its zone. Give a zone a soil moisture sensor and a threshold in %, 50 unless you set one, and while the reading is at or above it that zone sits the run out and the others water. Its duration for that run goes to 0 and its water balance is kept, so the deficit rolls over to the next run. Every calculation applies the same rule: a zone whose soil reads at or above its threshold has its water balance set to field capacity, so the deficit shown never contradicts the sensor between two starts. It works in that direction only. A dry reading says nothing about how many millimetres are missing without a calibration of the sensor to the soil, and a deficit invented from one would water a zone for good on the strength of a badly placed probe.

docs.title: Days between irrigation events
docs.text:
On the Skip watering page, the Days between irrigation card (under Settings > General before 2026.11.1; the setting is the same). Configure the minimum number of days that must pass between irrigation events. This setting allows you to control how frequently irrigation can occur, which is useful for: * Water conservation: Ensure adequate time between watering sessions * Plant health: Allow soil to partially dry between irrigations * Local restrictions: Comply with watering schedules or restrictions

How it works: * Default value: 0 (no restriction - maintains current behavior) * Range: 0-365 days * When set to 0: Irrigation events can fire daily if conditions are met (default behavior) * When set to a value > 0: Irrigation events will only fire if the specified number of days have passed since the last irrigation event

The value is the length of the watering cycle in calendar days: set to N, irrigation happens every N days.

Different days for one zone: a zone can have its own number of days, in the Days between irrigation field of the zone settings (advanced mode; once set, the field shows in every mode). The card lists the zones that have days of their own, each a link to its zone. That number replaces this general setting for that zone alone, so a lawn can wait three days while the flower beds are watered every day. Leave the zone's field empty to follow this setting. The general counter only restarts when a zone that follows it is watered, so a zone with days of its own, watered every day, does not keep the others from ever being due. The day is only skipped as a whole when every zone is still within its days; otherwise the run goes ahead for the zones that are due and the others sit it out.

Example scenarios: * Set to 1: Allow irrigation every day (one calendar day between events) * Set to 3: Allow irrigation every 3 days * Set to 7: Weekly irrigation

The system automatically tracks the number of days since the last irrigation event. The counter is incremented once per calendar day, at midnight, whether or not irrigation happened that day. If an irrigation trigger occurs but insufficient days have passed, the event is skipped and the counter simply keeps running. When enough days have passed, the next trigger will fire the irrigation event and reset the counter to 0.

This feature works alongside existing precipitation forecasting - if both restrictions apply, both must be satisfied for irrigation to occur.

docs.title: Zone configuration
docs.text:
Specify one or more irrigation zones here. The integration calculates irrigation duration per zone, depending on size, throughput, state, module and sensor group. A zone can be: * disabled: The zone is then not calculated and duration will be set to 0. * automatic: The zones duration is automatically calculated. * manual: You set the duration yourself, in minutes. Every start waters the zone for that duration, whatever its water balance, and a run keeps it.

When entering any values in the configuration of this integration, take notice of the labels provided so you enter values in the correct units.

docs.title: Multi-zone support
docs.text: For irrigation systems that have multiple zones which you want to run in series or independent you need to create multiple zones. The configuration should be done for each zone, including the area the zone covers and the corresponding settings.

docs.title: Adding a zone
docs.text:
You need to specify the following to add a zone:

  • Name: The name of your zone, e.g. 'garden'
  • Size: The size of this zone (m2 or sq ft)
  • Throughput: The flow of this zone (liter/minute or gallon/minute)

After entering the information, click Add zone to add the zone. Each zone is shown as an entity in Home Assistant. After adding a zone, make sure to further configure your new zone.

docs.title: Actions on all automatic Zones
docs.text: You can perform the following actions on all automatic zones: - Update all zones: Retrieve the weather data for all sensor groups for all automatic zones. - Calculate all zones: Calculate irrigation duration for all automatic zones. This will also delete weather data after calculation. - Reset all water balances: Set the water balances for all automatic zones to 0. - Clear all weatherdata: Remove all collected weather data for the sensor groups used by any automatic zone.

docs.title: Configuring a zone
docs.text:
To configure a zone, the amount of water that flows through the irrigation system (throughput) and the area the irrigation system reaches (size) must be known. If you do not know these values for your system, you can also directly enter the precipitation rate (in mm/h or in/h) for the zone. To determine the precipitation rate, place a straight-sided container in the zone, run the irrigation for exactly one hour, and measure the depth of water collected: that depth, in mm (or inches), is your precipitation rate per hour.

Every field of a zone has a short hint under it in the panel. For a manual zone, the line under the zone name shows its duration and litres; an automatic zone does not show it. The status band of an automatic zone reads the live estimate: "Short by X mm: about N min (V L) at the next calculation" when the estimate gives a duration, "Will water ... at the next start" when a stored duration exists, "Nothing to water" with the deficit under the zone's threshold, or "has what it needs".

You can change the following settings on a zone:

  • Name: change the name of a zone
  • Input method: choose how the zone's precipitation rate is determined:
  • Throughput & area (default): the rate is calculated from Size and Throughput.
  • Precipitation rate: enter the rate directly.
  • Size: change the size of a zone (only used with the Throughput & area input method)
  • Throughput: change the throughput of a zone (only used with the Throughput & area input method)
  • Precipitation rate: change the directly entered rate (only used with the Precipitation rate input method)
  • Drainage rate: how fast a saturated root zone drains, in mm/h, which is the soil's saturated hydraulic conductivity. It only applies when bucket > 0, meaning the soil is above field capacity. It is the full rate at saturation, when the water balance reaches the maximum water balance; below that it falls steeply with how much surplus is left, following Brooks and Corey, Eq. 4-6. The drainage over a calculation is worked out from that rate law exactly, so a surplus drains quickly at first and more and more slowly as it empties. Indicative values, from the texture-class averages in Rawls, Brakensiek and Saxton (1982): about 210 mm/h for sand, 60 for loamy sand, 26 for sandy loam, 13 for loam, 7 for silt loam, 2 for clay loam and under 1 mm/h for clay. A new zone starts at 8 mm/h, loam in the panel's soil list. Zones made earlier started at 50.8 mm/h, which is fast for most garden soils, and keep it. Either starting value reads as "Not chosen yet", with the number, until a soil is picked or a rate typed. The field appears right under Soil only when the soil is "I set the drainage myself", in both modes: a soil chosen by name stands for its rate. A drainage rate of 0 means a surplus never drains: rain above field capacity then stays in the water balance until evaporation removes it, and the next irrigation is delayed by however many days that takes.
  • State:
  • Automatic: Smart Irrigation calculates the duration from the water balance and waters at the start. It needs a sensor group.
  • Manual: waters only when asked, for the duration you typed. No sensor group required.
  • Disabled: never watered, and its balance is not followed.

  • Evapotranspiration: how this zone's water need is worked out, in three answers. Calculated by Smart Irrigation, from your measurements (temperature, humidity, wind, sun), which is FAO-56 Penman-Monteith. Provided by a sensor or a service, when you already have an evapotranspiration in millimetres and it is taken as it is. A fixed amount, so many mm a day whatever the weather. The module behind your answer is created and reused for you, one per zone; there is nothing to create by hand and no module to choose.

    On the advanced panel, the module's own setting appears with it: Look ahead, the number of days to come that are averaged into today's need (0 by default), for a zone calculated by Smart Irrigation, and the evaporation per day for a zone that uses a fixed amount, a positive number of mm the zone loses each day. Each zone has its own, so changing it here changes nothing anywhere else. - Sensor group: Choose the sensor group that provides the weather data for this zone. - Water balance: Either calculated or manually set. A negative water balance means the zone is short of water. If bucket >= 0 then no irrigation is necesarry, if bucket < 0 irrigation is necessary. See automations for examples on how to use this value to decide to irrigate. - Maximum water balance: how much water the root zone can hold above field capacity before it is saturated, so it only applies when bucket > 0. Anything beyond it runs off, and it is the saturation reference the drainage curve is scaled by. It is not the total water your soil holds for the plant, and it never changes when a zone starts watering.

    Physically it is (saturation - field capacity) x root depth: the soil's drainable porosity over the depth the roots use. The same averages give about 0.35 for sand, 0.19 for loam and 0.08 for clay, so for a 20 cm root zone roughly 70 mm for sand, 40 mm for loam and 15 mm for clay. Take them as a starting point: they move with how field capacity is defined, and a real soil is not a class average.

    Sand gets the larger value, not the smaller. Its big pores hold a lot of water for the short while it takes to drain and little once it has; clay is the reverse. Earlier versions of this page gave 30 mm for clay and 12 mm for sand. Those are closer to the available water capacity, which belongs to the other way of counting soil water, and they are inverted for this one. See discussion #783 for how this was worked out.

  • Lead time: Time needed to warm up your irrigation system (in seconds), e.g. time to establish a connection, start a pump, build pressure, etc. After the duration is calculated, the lead time is added but only if the duration is > 0.

  • Maximum duration: The maximum duration of the irrigation, to avoid flooding, wasting water, etc. When one run at this duration cannot make up what the zone loses between two waterings (a drip line capped at ten minutes with three days between waterings, say), Smart Irrigation raises a repair issue naming the zone: its deficit would otherwise grow for good. It is advice, and clears itself once the zone can keep up.

  • Crop factor (Kc): The factor between the reference evapotranspiration and what the planting uses. The field appears right under What grows here only when that choice is "I set the crop factor myself". It scales the evapotranspiration to the water your crop actually uses, ETc = ET0 * Kc, so the water balance is depleted at the crop's rate rather than the reference one. It is applied to the evapotranspiration and not to the rain that fell on it, nor to the resulting duration. For lawns, it is recommended to set the crop factor depending on your grass type (See this discussion for more details):

    • Cool-reason grasses (such as fescue, bluegrass) should be set to 0.8
    • Warm-season grasses (such as bermuda, zoysia) should be set to 0.7.

    It carries plant density too, not just species. The reference the calculation starts from is a continuous grass surface, so the figure quoted for a species assumes it covers the ground. A zone that does not is using less water per square metre than that figure says, because there is less leaf there to lose it. A hedge on a drip line, measured over the strip its emitters wet, is close to full cover once it has grown together and the species figure is about right. A young or widely spaced planting is not, and its factor should come down roughly in proportion to how much of the zone the canopy actually shades. The landscape literature writes this as the species factor multiplied by a density factor, which is the same idea.

This is why the area you enter and the crop factor have to describe the same patch of ground. If you take the whole bed as the area for a drip line, you are claiming a canopy over all of it; if you take the wetted strip, you are claiming one over the strip, which for an established hedge is true. Either can be made correct, but not by mixing one area with the other's factor.

A dry spell waters the same as it always did: the crop factor ends up multiplying the same total either way. What changes is a period with rain, where a factor below 1 used to credit only that fraction of the millimetres that fell and therefore over-watered, and the moment irrigation becomes necessary, which now arrives at the crop's rate of depletion rather than about 1/Kc times too early. - Soil: the soil of the zone by name (sandy, sandy loam, loam, clay loam, clay), which stands for its drainage rate (see Drainage rate above). Choose "I set the drainage rate myself" to type the rate. A zone nobody chose a soil for reads "Not chosen yet:" and its starting rate; choosing that again puts the zone back on 8 mm/h. - What grows here: the planting by name (lawn, vegetables, flowers, shrubs, hedge, fruit trees, vines, ground cover), which stands for its crop factor. Choose "I set the crop factor myself" to type the Crop factor (Kc) above. A zone nobody chose a planting for reads "Not chosen yet: factor 1.0". - Soil moisture sensor and Skip at or above (advanced mode; once a sensor is set, they show in every mode): a sensor of the soil of this zone and the % from which the zone sits out a run. See Skipping a run. - Linked valve/switch: the valve or switch that waters this zone. It is what observed watering watches, and what Smart Irrigation opens with Calculate and water. - Cumulative volume meter: a water-meter total for the zone, for exact crediting instead of throughput x time. See the volume meter. - Days between irrigation (advanced mode; once set, it shows in every mode): the minimum number of calendar days between two waterings of this zone alone. Empty, the default, follows the general days between irrigation setting, which is what every installation did before this field existed. A number replaces the general setting for this zone: 1 waters it every day it needs water, 3 at most every third day, 0 removes the restriction for it. The days are counted from the last time this zone was watered, and the zone's deficit keeps building while it waits, so it is made up at the next run. Useful when one garden holds a lawn that wants infrequent deep watering and flower beds that want water daily. - Crop factor by month (advanced mode): for a crop whose water use follows its growth, the crop factor (Kc) of each month, January first. A month left empty uses the crop factor of the zone, and twelve empty months are that crop factor all year, as before. A lawn can read 0.6 in March, 0.9 in June and 0.5 in November without a single adjustment to create. Seasonal adjustments still apply on top, as a multiplier of the factor of the month. - Available water and allowed depletion (advanced mode): what the soil of the zone holds for the plants, in mm, and the share of it the plants may use up before they suffer. Empty, the default, leaves the water balance exactly as it was: the deficit grows for as long as it does not rain. Set the available water (the root depth in metres times what the soil holds per metre of depth, about 50 to 110 mm for sand, 130 to 180 mm for loam and 120 to 200 mm for clay according to FAO-56, Table 19, so a lawn rooted at 0.15 m on loam holds about 20 to 27 mm) and two things change. The deficit cannot go below it, because a soil cannot be drier than that, and once the deficit passes the allowed share of it (50% unless you change it) the plants draw less water, falling to nothing as the soil empties (the FAO-56 stress coefficient). A zone watered in time never reaches that point, so the figure matters most after a long dry spell or a missed run, where it stops the water balance from showing a deficit no plant could have used. The threshold below stays in mm and is not tied to it. - Distribution efficiency (advanced mode): the share of the water leaving the emitters that reaches the plants, in %. Empty is 100%: the throughput is taken at its word, as before. A zone at 80% waters 25% longer for the same depth, and credits the water balance with only 80% of what it delivers, whether it is timed, observed or metered. Sprinklers in wind or on a slope lose some; drip loses almost none. - Irrigation threshold: how much of a soil moisture deficit to let build up before watering at all, in mm or inch. 0, the default, waters as soon as anything is missing, which is what every installation did before this setting existed; it is not what agronomy recommends for anything, a lawn included. Set a threshold and the zone stays dry until that much water is owed, then delivers all of it in one deep run: a lawn wants a small one because its roots are shallow, a tree or a hedge a large one. It changes when a zone waters, not how much: once the threshold is reached the run still covers the whole deficit. It follows that a zone never waters less than its threshold, so it also rules out very short runs. In soil terms this is the management allowed depletion (MAD).

To pick a value, work from the water your soil actually holds for the plant, the total available water: TAW = available water capacity of the soil x root depth. As a rough guide the available water capacity runs about 50 to 110 mm per metre in sand, 130 to 180 in loam and 120 to 200 in clay (FAO-56, Table 19), and the root depth is what matters for that planting, perhaps 0.15 to 0.3 m for turf and a metre or more for an established tree. The threshold is then a fraction of that, p x TAW, with p around 0.5 as a starting point (FAO-56 gives per-crop values, mostly between 0.4 and 0.6). A lawn on loam at 0.2 m therefore lands somewhere near 15 mm.

Do not derive it from the Maximum water balance: that setting caps the surplus above field capacity, which is the other side of zero and a different quantity entirely.

The default of 0 is there to keep existing installs behaving exactly as before, not because watering the instant anything is missing is good practice. Deep and infrequent watering suits a lawn too, it simply wants a smaller threshold than a tree because its roots are shallower. * view weather data. View the last 10 records of the associated sensor group. * view watering calendar. View a yearly watering calendar based on the location and normal weather patterns. * delete the zone.

docs.title: A zone in YAML
docs.text:
The Edit in YAML icon in a zone's header row shows its settings as text, in place of the form, and back, as for a program. The numbers are in the units the panel shows. Only settings are written: what the calculation and the runs write (water balance, duration, explanation, last calculation, measured throughput...) is not, and cannot be set there. An optional setting you remove is cleared; a required one (name, size, state...) is kept. Nothing is saved until Apply, which saves only what changed, the same way the form does; a key that is not a zone setting, or a value the zone refuses, is named under the editor.

name: Front lawn
state: automatic
size: 50
throughput: 12
linked_entity: valve.front_lawn
safety_off_topic: zigbee2mqtt/front_lawn_valve/set
safety_off_state_key: state_l1
open_resends: 0

YAML only: two zone options have no field in the form, even when they are set. Editing the zone in the form keeps them, and a zone that uses one says so in a Set in YAML (not editable here) box, with Edit in YAML at hand:

  • safety_off_state_key: state_l1, the safety off state key (empty is state);
  • open_resends: 0, how often the open is sent again while the valve has not confirmed (0 to 10; empty is the default).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: You use the Smart Irrigation panel to configure the integration. Make sure you install it first.

docs.title: Four tabs
docs.text:
The panel used to have ten tabs, which is nine more than most people open twice a year. It has four, each a group of pages: a group opens its first page and shows the others on a second row. Nothing was removed and every address still works.

  1. Home — what is happening. Info: what will happen at the next start and why, whether it would be held back, where each zone stands right now, and the days ahead. Then History: what actually ran, by day, with durations and volumes.
  2. Zones — the zones of your irrigation system: what each waters, how it is calculated, and what it is short of.
  3. Weather — where the numbers come from. Weather service with the location and how often it is read, sensor groups: which sensor or service provides each value the calculation reads, and the checks that skip a run on the weather.
  4. Settings — everything you set once. General: the master switch, then the calculation, the control and the system. Then Backup / restore, and Help.

Two pages are in no tab, and both are reachable.

  • The setup assistant is a button under Settings. It is for an installation that has nothing yet, so a tab inviting one that is already set up to set itself up was in the way.
  • The modules page is not in the navigation at all, because a zone says how it is calculated and the module behind that answer is created and reused for you. Its address still works and it appears under Settings while it is open.

docs.title: Standard and advanced
docs.text:
The panel comes in two depths, switched under Settings > General.

The standard panel keeps what a zone is: its name, what it waters with, where its weather comes from, what it is short of. The advanced panel adds the settings that tune the model — the drainage rate, the thresholds, the crop factor, how far ahead a zone looks, cycle and soak — which have sound defaults and are not improved by being met accidentally.

An installation that already had zones when this arrived is on the advanced panel, because those settings were chosen on purpose and folding them away would hide decisions its owner made. A fresh installation starts on the standard one. Either way the choice is yours from then on, and nothing is lost in either direction: the settings keep their values.

See also: Closed-loop watering, which lets Smart Irrigation credit the water balance from real irrigation and, optionally, drive the valves itself.

docs.title: From nothing to a watered garden
docs.text:
This is the whole path, for somebody who has none of it yet: a machine, a valve, Home Assistant, Smart Irrigation, and a zone that waters itself on what the weather took out of the soil. Half an hour of work, most of it waiting for downloads.

It is deliberately the shortest path that is still correct. Every step links to the page that goes deeper, and nothing here has to be undone later.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Something to run Home Assistant on. A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 is the usual answer, with a decent SD card or, better, an SSD. Any machine on Home Assistant's installation page works, including an old laptop or a virtual machine.

A way to open and close the water. Two routes, and the choice matters more than anything else on this page:

How it works Watch out for A wireless valve (Zigbee, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) Battery or mains valve that screws onto a tap and appears in Home Assistant as a valve or switch. Zigbee and Z-Wave need a coordinator stick. Battery life over a season, and range from the house to the garden. A relay board driving solenoid valves Irrigation solenoids (commonly 24 V AC) wired to a relay board, which Home Assistant switches. This is what a multi-zone garden ends up with. Mains and water in the same box: use a proper enclosure and a transformer rated for your valves, and have an electrician do it if you are not sure.

We do not sell or endorse hardware, and this page names no models on purpose: what matters is that the valve appears in Home Assistant as something you can turn on and off.

Weather data. No hardware needed: Open-Meteo is free and needs no account. Your own sensors are better if you have them, and you can add them later without starting over.

Numbers about your garden. Two, per zone, and you can measure them in ten minutes:

  • the area it waters, in m² or sq ft;
  • the flow, in litres or gallons per minute. Time how long your sprinkler takes to fill a bucket of known volume: a 10 litre bucket in 40 seconds is 15 L/min.

If you would rather not, the panel also takes a precipitation rate in mm/h directly, which is what a sprinkler manufacturer's data sheet gives.

docs.title: 1. Home Assistant (15 minutes, mostly unattended)
docs.text:
Follow Home Assistant's own installation guide for your machine and pick Home Assistant OS if you have the choice: it is the version that supports add-ons and updates itself, and it is the one every instruction you will read assumes.

On a Raspberry Pi, the steps are these. Home Assistant's own guide has the details and is the reference if anything differs.

  1. On another computer, install the Raspberry Pi Imager.
  2. In the Imager, choose your Pi model, then the operating system under Other specific-purpose OS, Home assistants and home automation, Home Assistant, and the version for your model. Choose the SD card or SSD, and write it. If you use an SSD, your Pi needs to be set up to boot from USB; the Imager and the Raspberry Pi documentation say how.
  3. Put the card or drive in the Pi, plug in the network cable (a cable is easier than Wi-Fi the first time) and the power. The first start downloads and prepares Home Assistant and takes a while, often twenty minutes. Nothing is wrong if the page is not there yet.
  4. From a computer on the same network, open http://homeassistant.local:8123 (or the Pi's address from your router) and follow the on-screen setup.

When it is up, create your account, set your location, time zone and elevation properly. Smart Irrigation needs them: the sun's position at your latitude is half of the evapotranspiration equation.

docs.title: 2. Your valve, in Home Assistant (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Add the valve the way its own integration asks (a Zigbee stick and ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT for a Zigbee valve, the brand's integration for a Wi-Fi one, a GPIO or Modbus integration for a relay board).

Then prove it works, before Smart Irrigation is anywhere near it: in Developer tools > Actions, call switch.turn_on (or valve.open_valve) on that entity and watch the water. Turn it off again. If that does not work, nothing later will, and it will look like our fault.

Write the entity id down, switch.garden_tap or whatever it is.

docs.title: 3. Smart Irrigation (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Install HACS if you do not have it, then:

  1. HACS > Integrations, search for Smart Irrigation, download it.
  2. Restart Home Assistant.
  3. Settings > Devices & services > Add integration, search for Smart Irrigation.
  4. Pick your weather service, or say you will use your own sensors. Open-Meteo needs nothing; OpenWeatherMap and Pirate Weather ask for a free API key.

The full version of this step, including the manual install and what to do when HACS does not find it, is on the installation page.

docs.title: 4. The first zone (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Open Smart Irrigation in the sidebar. The setup assistant asks four questions at most: what the zone is, whether it is outside or under glass, where the evaporation figure should come from, and which sensors you have. It creates the sensor group and the first zone for you.

Then, on the zone's card, fill in what only you know:

  • the area and the flow you measured;
  • what the soil is and what grows there, in words. Those two write the drainage rate and the crop factor behind them (FAO-56 values), which is what nobody can answer in millimetres an hour.

You now have a zone that computes a duration every night at 23:00.

docs.title: 5. Make the water actually flow (2 minutes)
docs.text:
This is the step people skip, and then nothing waters: Smart Irrigation decides how long, and something has to do it. Two ways.

Let Smart Irrigation do it. In Settings > General, choose Calculate and water in the first card, then set the zone's Linked valve/switch to the entity from step 2. It puts the zone in a program, which opens the valve at its schedule (done by sunrise unless you change it), waits the calculated duration, closes it, and credits the zone itself. Nothing else to write. Give your valve a hardware failsafe if it has one: if Home Assistant goes down mid-run, nothing here can close it.

Or keep your own automation. An import-ready blueprint does it for a plain switch, for Irrigation Unlimited, or for a Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler or B-hyve controller. Turn the controller's own schedule off if it has one, or it will water twice.

Either way, the Home page tells you whether an installation would ever water, and names the reason when it would not.

docs.title: 6. Check it, tonight and tomorrow
docs.text:
• Home page: what happens next, and what would hold it back. It answers in one sentence.
  • Press irrigate now on a zone, or add the dashboard card and press it there: two taps, and you should hear water.
  • Tomorrow morning, the zone's calculation explanation shows the night's numbers: what was read, what evaporated, what rain was credited, and the duration it produced.

docs.title: After a week
docs.text:
Change one thing at a time, and let a few days pass before judging it.

  • It waters too often, in short runs. Raise the zone's irrigation threshold: the deficit it lets build up before watering at all. Deep and infrequent is better for almost everything, a lawn included; the zones page has the arithmetic for picking a number from your soil and root depth.
  • It waters too much or too little overall. The crop factor is the honest knob (the what grows here choice sets it), not the duration. Check the flow you measured first.
  • The ground stays soaked. Your soil cannot take it that fast: water in several passes with a soak between them, under Settings > General on the advanced panel.
  • Nothing happens at all. Troubleshooting, then an issue with a diagnostics file, which is the fastest way to a real answer.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• How it works: the water balance, in plain terms.
  • Which weather service, and what each one gives you.
  • Zone configuration: every setting on a zone and what it does.
  • Closed loop: letting Smart Irrigation drive the valve, crediting from real runs, and cycle and soak.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
One word for each thing in the panel; these pages follow as they are revised. The code, the services, the entity ids and the attributes keep their names, so automations that use them don't change. The column "In code" gives that name.

When you translate the panel, use the word in the second or third column for the thing in the first; a language without a column yet is free to pick its word, as long as it keeps to one.

What it is Panel (English) Panel (German) In code The water a zone's root zone has, counted from field capacity, in mm (or inches). Zero means it holds what it can; below zero it is short, above zero there is a surplus that drains away. Water balance Wasserbilanz bucket What a zone is short of, the water balance below zero, as a positive amount. Deficit Defizit (negative bucket) The largest surplus a zone keeps above field capacity. Maximum water balance Maximale Wasserbilanz maximum_bucket How fast a saturated root zone drains, in mm/h. Drainage rate Entwässerungsrate drainage_rate The water lost to evaporation and plants. ET0 is the reference value from the weather, ETc that value times the crop factor. Evapotranspiration (ET0, ETc) Evapotranspiration (ET0, ETc) — The factor between ET0 and what the planting uses. Crop factor (Kc) Pflanzenfaktor (Kc) multiplier The way a zone's water loss is calculated: from the weather (PyETO), a fixed amount (Static), or a value another sensor provides (Passthrough). Module Modul module The sources a zone reads its weather from: a weather service, your own sensors, or both. Sensor group Sensorgruppe mapping An online service that provides weather data and forecasts. Weather service Wetterdienst weather_service How long a zone is watered at the next start, worked out from its water balance and its flow. Duration Dauer duration What starts the watering: a time, sunrise or sunset, or the sun's position. Start trigger Startauslöser irrigation_start_triggers A set of zones watered together on a schedule (full controller only). Program Programm programs Smart Irrigation opens and closes the valves itself. Full controller Volle Steuerung full_controller A soil or planting nobody picked: the zone is calculated with the value it started with. Not chosen yet Noch nicht gewählt soil_type / plant_type empty

docs.title: Words that are not used
docs.text:
Instead of Say bucket (in a text), Vorrat, Eimer water balance, Wasserbilanz engine, calculation engine, Berechnungs-Engine module, Modul mapping (in a text) sensor group, Sensorgruppe crop coefficient, multiplier, Pflanzenkoeffizient, Multiplikator crop factor, Pflanzenfaktor

"bucket" stays where it is code: the attribute bucket, the action set_bucket (and, until they go in 2027.11, set_all_buckets, reset_bucket and reset_all_buckets), and the entity ids ending in _bucket.

docs.text:
Start with the documentation: installation, configuration (zones, sensor groups, modules), usage, events, services and troubleshooting.

Prefer video? Watch the tutorial playlist on YouTube (English) or this community tutorial in German.

Still stuck? Browse the Discussions and the Home Assistant community thread.

docs.title: Help translate
docs.text:
The panel and the names Home Assistant shows for the integration (entities, buttons, services, the setup dialog) come in 20 languages. Apart from English and French, those translations were machine-made and nobody who speaks the language has read them yet, so some will read oddly.

If yours does, you can fix it on Hosted Weblate, in the browser: pick the language, correct the string, save. No Git, no build tools. The corrections reach the repository as a pull request and ship with the next release. One word in one string is a welcome contribution.

A few rules keep a translation working, and Weblate checks most of them for you:

  • Keep every placeholder as it is, such as {count} or {duration}: the integration fills them in.
  • Reuse the words the panel already uses for the same idea, so a user reads one word on every screen.
  • Leave a string untranslated rather than guess. An untranslated string shows in English, an empty one shows nothing.

Your language is not in the list? Ask on Weblate or open an issue: a new language needs a small change in the panel as well as its translation. Prefer editing the files directly? The contribution guide explains how.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The below image shows a graphical representation of what this integration does.

The words for each part, as the panel uses them, are in the glossary.

  1. Snow and rain fall on the ground add moisture. Together, this makes up the precipitation.
  2. Sunshine, temperature, wind speed, place on earth and other factors influence the amount of moisture lost from the ground(evapotranspiration).
  3. The difference between precipitation and evapotranspiration is the delta or nett precipitation: negative values mean more moisture is lost than gets added by rain/snow, while positive values mean more moisture is added by rain/snow than what evaporates.
  4. At some point in the day (configurable) the nett precipitation is added/substracted from the water balance (the bucket attribute), which starts at zero. The water balance is calculated using this formula: `old_bucket + nett precipitation.
  5. If the water balance > 0, the drainage rate is taken into the account (if set) and subtracted from the water balance value. The actual drainage rate is determined dynamically by the fraction the water balance is of the maximum water balance value, following hydraulic conductivity method of Brooks and Corey, Eq. 4-6. When it rained during the window, the window is replayed hour by hour: each hour gets its evapotranspiration, the rain that fell in it, then that hour's drainage. The evapotranspiration of each hour is the hourly equation's own figure when the hourly calculation is on, and otherwise follows the sun (in proportion to how high it stands, nothing at night). A rain that just fell is only drained from the hour it fell, not as if it had been in the soil since the previous calculation. When the rain is seen is taken from the readings of the rain sensor (a rain gauge's total, or a rain rate); when nothing says it, the rain is spread evenly over the window.
  6. If the water balance is below zero, irrigation is required.
  7. Irrigation should run for sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] seconds, which is 0 when bucket >= 0 or when the deficit is below the zone's irrigation threshold — deep and infrequent beats a daily trickle.
  8. Afterwards the water balance has to be credited with the water that went in. Three ways, and you pick one: let Smart Irrigation open the valve itself, which credits the run it performed; let it watch the valve and credit any run of it; or call credit_watering from your own automation with how long the zone ran. Never two of them, or the water is counted twice. A blueprint does the third for you, per brand of controller.

The whole of what is published and when it changes is on one page: the output contract.

docs.title: What the crop needs, not what a lawn of grass would
docs.text:
The evapotranspiration the equation computes is a reference: what a short, well-watered grass surface would lose. A hedge, a vegetable bed and a lawn do not lose the same, and the difference is the crop factor Kc, which is the zone's crop factor setting:

ETc = ET0 x Kc

It is applied to the evapotranspiration, before the water balance. That order matters, and it is worth saying why, because it used to be the other way round: the factor was applied at the very end, to the duration. That scaled the whole balance rather than the crop's water use, so a factor below 1 credited only that fraction of the rain that fell, and the water balance kept draining at the full reference rate — reaching any threshold about 1/Kc times too fast. No factor applied at the end can undo a decision about when to water.

The panel asks what grows in the zone, in words, and writes the FAO-56 factor for the answer. Your own number wins if you set one.

docs.title: Hour by hour, or once a day
docs.text:
The equation exists in two forms, and both are FAO-56.

The daily form runs once over the whole window, on its averages. The hourly form prices each hour of the window and adds them up. They are not the same number, because evapotranspiration is not linear in its terms: a cool humid night and a hot dry afternoon priced separately do not give what their averages give, and the separate answer is the right one. The daily equation is an average of a curve.

A new installation starts on the hourly form. One that existed before it arrived keeps the daily one until its owner switches, because the two give different numbers and nobody's watering should change on an update. The switch is under Settings > General, and what each form needs is documented there.

Either way the sun is the term the result is most sensitive to. A radiation sensor is best, a weather service that publishes radiation is next, and the day's temperature range is the last resort — the estimate FAO-56 gives for exactly that case.

docs.title: Weekly behavior example
docs.text: To understand how precipitation, nett precipitation, the water balance and irrigation interact, see let's look at an example behavior in a week. With this you should be able to do a sanity check against your confiruation and make sure everything is working together. The scenario is as follows: we will look at several days, including the precipitation and evapotranspiration for those days and the effects on the water balance and whether ot not irrigation should be triggered. Note that the values here are not representative of any real-life situation and the example below only uses one zone to keep things simple.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text: Initially, the water balance is 0, so the duration for irrigation is set to 0s.

docs.title: Variables used
docs.text:
• P: Precipitation
  • Et: Evapotranspiation
  • D: nett Precipitation or Delta (=P-Et)
  • B: Water balance
  • Bu: Water balance after calculation has happened (=B+D)
  • Du: Duration for irrigation in seconds

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Day P Et D B Bu Du Notes 1 0.5 0.1 0.4 0 0.4 0 P > Et so water balance increased from 0 to 0.4. Since Bu > 0 no irrigation is required 2 0 0.6 -0.6 0.40 -0.2 180 P < Et, so water balance decreased from 0.4 to -0.2. Since Bu < 0` irrigation is required and water balance is reset afterwards 3 1 0.2 0.8 0 (reset) 0.8 0 No irrigation required 4 0.2 0.4 -0.2 0.8 0.6 0 No irrigation required even though P < Et and water balance was decreased from 0.8 to 0.6 5 0 1.5 -1.5 0.6 -0.9 600 Since Bu < 0 irrigation is required and water balance is reset afterwards 6 0 0.4 -0.4 0 (reset) -0.4 300 Since Bu < 0 irrigation is required and water balance is reset afterwards 7 0.5 0.2 0.3 0 (reset) 0.3 0 No irrigation required

docs.title: When to irrigate
docs.text: You should irrigate when the irrigation tells you to, but keep in mind that for grass, experts say you should water deeply but infrequently to avoid overwatering and encourage deep rooting. It might be a good idea to create an automation that starts early enough to finish before sunrise and run that only once per week if duration is 0 or if the bucket < -25 mm (~1"). Adjust to your specific needs. See Example automation for examples.

docs.title: Installation: Download
docs.text:
1. Install the custom integration using HACS or manually:

    • Using HACS (recommended): Smart Irrigation is in the HACS default store, and HACS handles updates. Open it in HACS in one click:

    or search for Smart Irrigation in the HACS panel. Then click Download. If you added this repository as a custom repository in the past, that entry is no longer needed. * Manually: Download the latest release as a zip file and extract it into the custom_components folder of your Home Assistant configuration (you should end up with custom_components/smart_irrigation/).

  2. Restart Home Assistant to load the integration.

  3. Go to Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration, search for Smart Irrigation and click to add it.
  4. Confirm with OK: setup asks nothing. Then open the Smart Irrigation panel, where the setup assistant creates a first zone with you and the weather service is chosen.

docs.title: Installation: Migration from V1 (0.0.X) to V2 (202X.X.X)
docs.text:
Version 2 (202X.X.X) presents a complete rewrite of the integration compared to V1 (0.0.X). Everything was done from scratch. Many bugs present in V1 are fixed in V2. On top of that V2 provides multi zone support and overall better performance, more accurate results and more flexibility to configure the system to your needs. Also, in version 2 only one instance of Smart Irrigation is allowed. In V1, if you wanted multiple zones you needed to install multiple instances of Smart Irrigation.

docs.title: Installation: Options
docs.text:
Everything is set in the Smart Irrigation panel, in the sidebar. The integration's Configure button (Settings > Devices & services > Smart Irrigation) only says so.

  • The location the weather is read for is Home Assistant's, unless you give other coordinates on the Location coordinates card, on the Weather service page of the Weather tab. The card shows in the advanced mode, or whenever manual coordinates are on. See manual coordinates.
  • The weather service and its API key: see Configuring the weather service.

Up to 2026.11.0, Configure asked for manual coordinates, but what it saved was never used: the weather was always read for the coordinates of the panel's card. If you set coordinates there, set them again on the card.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
To remove Smart Irrigation from Home Assistant, go to Configuration > Integrations. In the Smart Irrigation card, click the button with the 3 dots, and click 'Delete'.

Deleting it removes its zones, sensor groups, programs and settings. Adding it again starts from nothing, with the setup assistant. If you may want them back, export a backup first under Settings › Backup / restore in the Smart Irrigation panel.

To remove all files, do the following: * If installed with HACS: in the HACS panel, find Smart Irrigation. Click the button with the 3 dots and click 'Uninstall'. * If installed manually: in the custom_components directory, remove the smart_irrigation folder.

Restart HA to remove all traces of the integration from your sytem.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
1. To install the latest version, follow these instructions:
    • If installed using HACS: In the HACS panel or in the Home Assistant updates there should be a notification when a new version is available. Follow the instructions within HACS to update the installation files. You can also force checking for an update by updating information for the repository in the HACS.
    • If installed manually: Download the latest release as a zip file and extract it into the custom_components folder in your Home Assistant installation, overwriting the previous installation.
  2. To install a specific version, follow these instructions:
    • If installed using HACS: depending on the HACS version you are using you can either use find a version dropdown in the Redownload option or you have to use the update.install service as follows: 
      action: update.install
target:
  entity_id: update.smart_irrigation_update
data:
  version: v2026.10.2
    • If installed manually: Download the zip file for the specific release you want and extract it into the custom_components folder in your Home Assistant installation, overwriting the previous installation.
  3. Restart HA to load the changes.
  4. (Optional) Verify the version number:
    • Verify version of the backend: In HA, go to Configuration -> Integrations. In the Smart Irrigation card, click the device to see the Device info. The 'firmware version' represents the installed version number.
    • Verify version of the frontend: In the Smart Irrigation configuration panel, the version number is displayed in the top right. If the version does not match with the backend version, your browser has an outdated version stored in the cache. To clear the cache, you should do a force refresh of your browser.

docs.title: Configuring the weather service
docs.text:
The weather service is configured from the Smart Irrigation panel, on the fly — it is no longer part of the install wizard. You can enable it, change it, or turn it off at any time without reinstalling or reloading the integration.

To set it up:

  1. Open the Smart Irrigation panel from the Home Assistant sidebar.
  2. Go to the Weather service settings.
  3. Toggle Use a weather service on, then pick the service you want:
  4. Open-Meteo (the default) is keyless and works worldwide — no API key required.
  5. A weather entity in Home Assistant reads one of your weather entities (DWD, Met.no, KNMI, ...): pick the entity instead of a key. It reports no rain that fell, so each sensor group needs a rain sensor (see weather services).
  6. Open Weather Map and Pirate Weather require an API key (see below).
  7. Enter the API key if the chosen service needs one, or pick the weather entity, then save. When the key or the entity is accepted you will see a success message; otherwise double check it. After switching to a weather entity, the page also names the sensor groups that still take their rain from the weather service: give each of them a rain sensor.

If you turn the weather service off, forecasting is unavailable and you must provide all weather data from another source, such as your own weather station sensors, configured in your sensor groups.

Make sure your Home Assistant home location is set correctly so the data matches your location, or set manual coordinates.

docs.title: Getting Open Weather Map API Key
docs.text: Go to OpenWeatherMap and create an account. You can enter any company and purpose while creating an account. After creating your account, You will need to sign up for the paid (but free for limited API calls) OneCall API 3.0 plan if you do not have a key already. Make sure to enter credit card information to get the API truly activated. Then, go to API Keys and get your key. If the key does not work right away, no worries. The email you should have received from OpenWeaterMap says it will be activated 'within the next couple of hours'. So if it does not work right away, be patient a bit. If you are worried about the cost of the API, You can put a rate limit below the paid threshold in the "Billing plans" page of your profile.

docs.title: Getting Pirate Weather API key
docs.text: Follow the instructions on this page (see API Key section): https://docs.pirateweather.net/en/latest/API/.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Starting with nothing at all, not even Home Assistant? From nothing to a watered garden walks the whole path in half an hour, hardware included, and comes back here for this part.

Smart Irrigation needs Home Assistant 2026.3 or later.

Installing the Smart Irrigation integration consists of a few steps:

  1. Downloading the integration.
  2. Adding it in Home Assistant. Setup is a single step that asks nothing: the weather service, the sensor groups and the zones are set up afterwards in the panel, by its setup assistant.

After the integration has been installed, you will find a new panel named 'Smart Irrigation' in your side bar. Use it to configure your set up.

Then choose where your weather data comes from:

  1. Configuring the weather service (done from the panel, on the fly).

Also in this section:

  1. Options: the Configure button
  2. Updating to the latest or specific version
  3. Migration from V1 (v0.0.X) to V2 (202X.X.X)
  4. Uninstalling the integration

docs.title: Assistants (AI)
docs.text:
Smart Irrigation can be offered to an assistant: Claude, ChatGPT or any other client of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or a conversation agent of Home Assistant (Assist). The assistant can then answer questions such as "why was the lawn not watered this morning?", "what will run tomorrow?" or "which zone is the driest?", and set Smart Irrigation up with you: "add a zone for the vegetable garden on the second valve", "water the hedges every other evening".

There is nothing to turn on in Smart Irrigation: it offers itself to Home Assistant (an API of Home Assistant's LLM helper, no server of its own), and no assistant sees it until you pick it there. Whatever it is asked, the assistant never runs a watering and never opens a valve.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• With an MCP client: add Home Assistant's own Model Context Protocol Server integration (Settings, Devices & services, Add integration) and tick Smart Irrigation in its options. Connect the client to Home Assistant as that integration's page explains; Home Assistant does the authentication.
  • With Assist: in the options of your conversation agent, tick Smart Irrigation among the APIs it may use.

Untick it there and the assistant no longer reaches Smart Irrigation.

docs.title: What the assistant can read
docs.text: Tool What it gives GetZones Each zone: state, water balance (mm, a deficit when negative), next duration, valve, size, throughput, lead time, sensor group. GetZoneSettings Every stored setting of one zone (metric). GetIrrigationInfo The next watering and why a zone is held back or skipped, as on the Home tab. GetPrograms The programs of the full controller, their steps (zones by id and by name) and schedules. GetPlanning What the programs will water over the next days (1 to 14), each run's zones in order and whether the weather is expected to hold it back. GetSensorGroups The sensor groups (where each weather input comes from) and the calculation modules. GetSettings The general settings, in the unit system of Home Assistant, with mode first. FindEntities The valves, switches, sensors and weather entities of Home Assistant, with their unit, device class and the make and model of their device: what the assistant needs to ask you the right questions. PreviewProgram A program as the assistant wrote it, cleaned the way a save cleans it and dry-run on the zones as they are now: each zone's start, end and water, the total, and the zones it could not find. Nothing is saved. GetConfigReference Every field the assistant can write, for a program, its steps, schedules and notifications, and for a zone: type, allowed values or range, unit, default and meaning. The options set only in YAML are flagged yaml_only.

docs.title: What it can change
docs.text:
Tool What it does SaveZone, DeleteZone Create a zone, change its settings, or delete it. SaveSensorGroup, DeleteSensorGroup Create a sensor group, change where its inputs come from, or delete it. SaveSettings Change general settings: mode, what Smart Irrigation does (water, calculate or off, the list at the top of Settings), then calculation, skip conditions, start triggers, sequencing, passes and soak, pumps... The switches mode replaced are refused one by one. SaveProgram, DeleteProgram Add or replace a program, or delete one. A program that names a zone that does not exist is refused.

Every change goes through the path the panel saves with, so the same checks apply: a zone cannot be linked to one of Smart Irrigation's own valves, an unknown setting is refused, a program is cleaned the same way. The assistant is told to say what it is about to change, and most clients ask you before a tool that writes; deleting is marked as such. Each change is written in Home Assistant's log (An assistant saved zone 3, at the info level).

docs.title: Writing a program together
docs.text:
Ask for the program you want ("water the vegetable garden and the greenhouse together every other evening, then the hedges"). The assistant writes it in the YAML shape of the program editor, checks it with PreviewProgram and gives it to you. Paste it in Watering, Programs, with Edit in YAML on a New program or on an existing one: the timeline shows what it would do before you apply it.

The assistant does not have to guess the fields: GetConfigReference lists every one a program, a step, a schedule and a zone can be written with, the YAML-only options included (a step's adjust_seconds, a schedule's months or fallback_time...), with their range and default. So it can set an option the panel's form has no field for, and that no program of yours uses yet.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: The assistant receives what these tools return: zone names, entity ids and the names and models of your devices, the weather-based figures and the schedules. With a cloud assistant, that leaves your home. Do not tick Smart Irrigation in the MCP server or the conversation agent if you do not want that.

docs.title: Automations
docs.text:
Since this integration does not interface with your irrigation system directly, you will need to use the data it outputs to create an automation that will start and stop your irrigation system for you. This way you can use this custom integration with any irrigation system you might have, regardless of how that interfaces with Home Assistant. In order for this to work correctly, you should base your automation on the value of sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] as long as you run your automation after it was updated (e.g. 11:00 PM/23:00 hours local time). If that value is above 0 it is time to irrigate. Note that the value is the run time in seconds. Also, after irrigation, you need to call the smart_irrigation.credit_watering service with how long the zone ran, so the water balance is credited with the water it received. (smart_irrigation.set_bucket without a value, which sets the water balance to 0, still works, but loses the deficit a run cut short by the maximum duration did not water.)

The last step in any automation is very important, since you will need to let the integration know you have finished irrigating, by calling the smart_irrigation.credit_watering service

Resetting the water balance says the soil is at field capacity at that moment, so any rain collected since the last calculation is part of what that statement covers and is not counted again at the next one. Rain falling after the reset still counts as usual. This matters when it rains between the calculation and irrigation: without it the same rain would both shorten the run and be counted again in the next water balance.

Experts say you should water deeply but infrequently to avoid overwatering and encourage deep rooting. It might be a good idea to create an automation that starts early enough to finish before sunrise (using the smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones event) and only once per week if duration is above 0 or whenever the bucket < -25 mm. Adjust to your specific needs.

The examples on this page don't use a timer - see this discussion for an example of using a timer for extra safety.

Writing your own executor rather than using a blueprint? The output contract says exactly what Smart Irrigation publishes, when it changes, and what to send back.

docs.title: Blueprints we provide
docs.text:
A blueprint is a parameterised mould for an automation: you import it once, pick your entities from filtered dropdowns, and Home Assistant writes the automation for you.

You already have them. Smart Irrigation copies the blueprints below into your own blueprints/ folder when it starts, so they are waiting for you under Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints, grouped as Smart Irrigation. Nothing to download.

Existing files are never overwritten, so anything you have edited stays yours. That also means an improved blueprint does not reach you on its own: use the Import link in the table below to pull the current version. Each blueprint is copied once: one you delete is not put back at the next start. To copy none at all, switch off Install the example blueprints in the Blueprints card of the General page (advanced mode); the ones already in your folder are left as they are. You can also browse the whole folder.

Pick the one that matches how your valves are actually driven:

Blueprint Use it when standard-irrigation.yaml A plain switch, valve or input_boolean per zone. Turns it on for the calculated duration, then credits the run to the water balance (credit_watering). Has an optional pause switch. Import esphome.yaml An ESPHome device that takes the duration itself. Import simple-scheduler.yaml A script rather than an automation, if you prefer to call irrigation from elsewhere. Import irrigation-unlimited-adjust-time-single-zone.yaml Irrigation Unlimited runs your schedule and you want Smart Irrigation to set the run time of one zone through adjust_time. Import irrigation-unlimited-adjust-time-sequence.yaml The same for one zone inside an IU sequence. Adjusting a sequence as a whole spreads the time across its zones in proportion to their original durations, which is not what a calculated duration means, so this adjusts one zone of it and you add one automation per zone. Import irrigation-unlimited-reset-bucket.yaml Pair with either of the two above: resets the water balance when IU reports the run finished. Import weather-responsive-scheduling.yaml You want a seasonal multiplier applied automatically and runs skipped on cold or windy days. Import valve-watchdog.yaml A backstop: closes a valve left open longer than a limit you set, and tells you. Worth adding whatever else you use. Import rainbird.yaml A Rain Bird controller: starts the Rain Bird zone for the calculated run, in whole minutes. Import hydrawise.yaml A Hunter Hydrawise controller: the same, through hydrawise.start_watering. Import rachio.yaml A Rachio controller: the same, through rachio.start_watering (at most 3 hours a run). Import opensprinkler.yaml An OpenSprinkler controller (the OpenSprinkler integration from HACS): the run in seconds, through opensprinkler.run_station. Import bhyve.yaml An Orbit B-hyve controller (the B-hyve integration from HACS), through bhyve.start_watering. Import

With an off-the-shelf controller (Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler, B-hyve), Smart Irrigation decides how long each zone waters and the controller runs the valves. The off-the-shelf controllers page walks through the setup, which entity to pick for each brand, how to turn off the controller's own schedule, and what to do with several zones. These five have been written against each integration's documented actions but not yet confirmed on real hardware: if you have one, a word on the discussions saying it works, or what it needed, is the most useful contribution there is.

Irrigation-V5 needs no blueprint at all: it reads a numeric entity as a multiplier, so pointing its Adjustment Sensor at our zone sensor with a base watering time of 1 second gives it the calculated duration directly. See executor integration.

With Irrigation Unlimited, note that it exposes binary sensors, not switches: Smart Irrigation tells it how long to run through adjust_time and IU does the running. Do not drive the valve yourself in parallel, or the two will fight.

If you use observed watering or Calculate and water (see closed loop), turn off the blueprint's option "Credit the run to the water balance" (the Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler and B-hyve blueprints have it; the standard one always credits, so leave it out): the integration credits the water balance itself and the two would count twice. The ESPHome blueprint, the simple-scheduler script, the Irrigation Unlimited reset blueprint and the example automations below still call set_bucket without a value, which sets the water balance to 0 instead of crediting the run.

docs.title: Example 1: one valve, once per week irrigation if duration > 0 or if the water balance < - 25 mm:
docs.text:
This example automation runs daily and checks sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name]. It checks if the buckets is < -25mm (~1") or if's a monday and duration is above 0. This follows the expert recommendation mentioned above.

yaml

docs.title: Example 2: one valve, potentially daily irrigation
docs.text:
Here is an example automation that runs when the smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones event is fired. It checks if sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] is above 0 and if it is it turns on switch.irrigation_tap1, waits the number of seconds as indicated by sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] and then turns off switch.irrigation_tap1. Finally, it resets the water balance by calling the smart_irrigation.set_bucket service without a value. If you have multiple instances you will need to adjust the event, entities and service names accordingly.

yaml

docs.title: Example 3: one valve, irrigation depending on work day sensor
docs.text:
Here is an example automation that runs at 5 AM local time, but only on set days of the week indicated by binary_sensor.workday_sensor). As above, it checks if sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] is above 0 and if it is it turns on switch.irrigation_tap1, waits the number of seconds as indicated by sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] and then turns off switch.irrigation_tap1. Finally, it resets the water balance by calling the smart_irrigation.set_bucket service without a value. This automation depends on the workday binary sensor which you will have to set up separately. Alternatively you could use a condition such as: 

condition:
  condition: time
  weekday:
  - mon
  - thu

yaml

docs.title: Example 4: two valves, irrigation depending on work day sensor
docs.text:
Here is an example automation that runs at 4 AM local time, but only on set days of the week indicated by binary_sensor.workday_sensor). As above, it checks if sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] is above 0 and if it is it turns on switch.irrigation_tap1, waits the number of seconds as indicated by sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] and then turns off switch.irrigation_tap1. Then it turns on switch.irrigation_tap2, waits the number of seconds as indicated by sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name] and then turns off switch.irrigation_tap2. Finally, it resets the water balance by calling the smart_irrigation.set_bucket service without a value. This automation depends on the workday binary sensor which you will have to set up separately. Alternatively you could use a condition such as: 

condition:
  condition: time
  weekday:
  - mon
  - thu

yaml

docs.text:
This example handles multiple taps for a six-zone system controlled by ESPHome. This is the automation the creator of this integration uses themselves (ignoring the expert advice above...).

docs.title: The dashboard card
docs.text: The panel in the sidebar is where an installation is set up, which is occasional work. The card is for the rest of the time: it sits on your dashboard, next to the lights, and says what each zone is short of, how long it would run, and when the water goes on.

docs.title: Adding it
docs.text:
Nothing to install. The integration serves the card and registers it with Lovelace itself, so it is already in the card picker:

  1. Open the dashboard you want it on and press the pencil to edit it.
  2. Add card, then look for Smart Irrigation in the list (searching for "irrigation" finds it).
  3. Set it up in the editor that opens, and save.

If your dashboards are written in YAML, resources are yours to manage and the integration does not touch them. Add this once, under lovelace: resources:, and the log line at startup gives you the exact URL:

resources:
  - url: /api/smart_irrigation/card.js
    type: module

Then put type: custom:smart-irrigation-card in a view.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• The next start, and when a run would be held back, the reason it would be: rain in the forecast, freezing, wind, or a rain sensor that says it is raining.
  • Per zone: the water it is short of, the run that would deliver it, and when it last watered. A zone in manual or disabled state says so next to its name.
  • A zone that would water now is in the accent colour, so a glance is enough.

The deficit is the live estimate, not last night's result. The integration re-runs the same calculation over the readings collected since the zone's last one, without committing anything, and the card shows that with a small icon at the end of the line; hovering it says what the estimate is measured from. A zone calculated minutes ago has nothing new to add, and then the card shows its committed value.

The estimate is computed on the server for every zone, so the card asks for it every two minutes, and not at all while you are looking at another tab or another window. Coming back to it refreshes it at once.

docs.title: The buttons
docs.text: Button What it does Water now (drop) Runs that zone's valve for the calculated duration, and credits the water balance when it finishes. It takes two taps: the first arms it, the second runs it, and it disarms itself after five seconds. It only appears for a zone that has a linked valve, and only with Calculate and water. Calculate (calculator) Runs the calculation for that zone now and commits it, as the panel's own button does. Start (play) On a program row: runs the program now, or as soon as it is its turn. Only on an idle program. Pause / Resume On a running or paused program: holds the watering and goes on from where it stopped. Pause calls the global pause_watering service, so it holds all the watering, not one program, and ends by itself after the service's default of 60 minutes if nobody resumes. Next step (skip) Ends the zones of the step in progress and goes on to the next step. Stop (square) Stops the watering and closes the valves. It takes two taps, like Water now.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text:
When the full controller is on and has programs, a block above the zones lists one row per program: its name, its state (idle, running, waiting, paused, suspended or disabled) and its next start. While a program runs, the row shows the step (for example 2/3), the percentage done and the time left. The card asks for this every 5 seconds while a program is running, paused or waiting, and every 60 seconds otherwise, and not at all while the tab is hidden. With the full controller off, or no program, nothing is shown and the card looks as before. Hide the block with show_programs: false.

Stop acts on the whole watering, not on one program, because the controller waters one program at a time.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
All of them are in the visual editor, and this is what they are called in YAML:

Option Default What it does title Smart Irrigation The card's header. zones every zone The zone ids to show. Use it for a card per area, or to keep the greenhouse on its own dashboard. show_next_start true The next start line above the zones. compact false Only the zones that would water now. The card then says "Nothing to water right now" when none would. show_programs true The programs block, shown only when the full controller is on and has at least one program. Set it to false to hide it. 
type: custom:smart-irrigation-card
title: Garden
zones: [0, 2]
compact: true

The card reads its words from the language files, with English as the fallback. The programs block is translated in all 20 languages.

docs.title: A card from the community
docs.text: Irrigation Zone Card, by @lweberru, is a visual card for one zone at a time: the soil moisture as a ring, the live water balance on a scale with its zero point, the calculated duration, the water used and an optional valve control; the same installation adds Irrigation Overview, a card for the planning, rain and frost protection and the integration-wide actions. It finds a zone's entities from the integration's stable ids, so renamed entities keep working. It is installed from HACS as a custom repository (type Dashboard) and maintained by its author; questions about it go to its repository.

docs.title: Off-the-shelf controllers
docs.text:
If your valves are wired to a commercial controller, you do not have to replace it. Smart Irrigation decides how long each zone waters, and the controller runs the valves, through the action its Home Assistant integration provides. One blueprint per controller does the plumbing:

Controller Integration Action the blueprint calls Unit Longest run Rain Bird Rain Bird (built in) rainbird.start_irrigation minutes 1440 min Hunter Hydrawise Hydrawise (built in) hydrawise.start_watering minutes 1440 min Rachio Rachio (built in) rachio.start_watering minutes 180 min OpenSprinkler hass-opensprinkler (HACS) opensprinkler.run_station seconds 64800 s Orbit B-hyve bhyve-home-assistant (HACS) bhyve.start_watering minutes 1440 min

This is different from Calculate and water, where Smart Irrigation opens and closes a switch or valve entity itself. A controller does not expose its zones that way: you hand it a duration, it starts its own timer and stops on its own. That is what the blueprints do.

These blueprints have not yet been confirmed on real hardware. They were written against each integration's documented actions and their templates are rendered by Home Assistant's own module in our tests, but we do not own the controllers. If you do, a word in the discussions saying it works, or what it needed, is the most useful contribution there is.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Smart Irrigation calculates. At least one zone is in automatic mode and the Home page shows a duration for it after the daily calculation.
  2. A start trigger is set on the General page. The blueprints listen to the smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones event; without a trigger, that event never fires and nothing waters.
  3. The controller's integration is set up in Home Assistant and its zones show up as entities.
  4. The controller's own schedule is off for the zones Smart Irrigation will drive. Otherwise it waters twice: once on its own program, once on ours. How to do that for each brand is below.

docs.title: Set up one zone
docs.text:
The blueprints are copied into your own blueprints/ folder when the integration starts, so they are already in Home Assistant. If you do not see them, or want the latest version, use the import links on the automations page.

  1. Go to Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints and pick Smart Irrigation with Rain Bird (or Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler, B-hyve).
  2. Click Create automation and fill in the three fields:
  3. Smart Irrigation zone: the zone's duration sensor, sensor.smart_irrigation_<zone name>. The list only offers Smart Irrigation duration sensors.
  4. Controller zone: the entity of the controller zone that waters it. Which entity that is depends on the brand, see the notes below. The list is filtered to that integration.
  5. Credit the run to the water balance: leave it on, unless observed watering already watches this controller zone. In that case turn it off, or the run is credited twice.
  6. Save, give the automation the zone's name, and repeat for every zone.

One automation per zone is deliberate: each zone has its own duration and its own water balance.

docs.title: What happens at run time
docs.text:
When the start trigger is reached, every automation created from these blueprints wakes up at the same moment and does the same thing:

  1. Checks the duration. If the zone's duration is 0, nothing happens. On a skip day the start event is not fired at all, so nothing happens either.
  2. Converts the duration to what the controller takes. Smart Irrigation counts in seconds. Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio and B-hyve take whole minutes, so the run is rounded up (a calculated 3 min 10 s becomes 4 min: a little too much water is better than a deficit left behind) and is at least 1 minute. OpenSprinkler takes seconds and gets them as they are. Every run is capped at the longest run the controller accepts, see the table above. Rachio's cap of 3 hours is the one you may actually hit: if a zone regularly needs more, check its throughput and precipitation rate on the zones page.
  3. Starts the controller zone for that time. The controller runs its own timer and stops the valve itself.
  4. Waits the same time, then credits the run to the water balance of the zone (the credit_watering action, with the time it ran), so the next calculation starts from what the soil really received. A run cut short by the zone's maximum duration keeps the deficit it did not water. If you turned the credit off, the automation just ends.
