The automation runs in single mode: a second start event while a run is in progress is ignored.

The controller's own rain sensor or rain delay. If your controller cancels or shortens a run on its own (a wired rain sensor, a rain delay set in the app), the blueprint does not know: it waits the full time and credits the water balance as if the water had gone in. Two ways to keep the books right. Either turn that feature off on the controller and let Smart Irrigation decide, since it already accounts for rain, or use observed watering on the controller zone and turn the blueprint's credit off, so the water balance is credited with what actually ran.

docs.title: Several zones
docs.text:
All the automations start at the same event, so the controller is asked to start every zone at once. What happens next is the controller's business:

  • OpenSprinkler queues the runs and waters the zones one after the other.
  • Rachio and Hydrawise normally run one zone at a time; check in the app what your controller does when a second zone is asked to start while one is running.
  • Rain Bird and B-hyve: same advice, check the app.

If your controller refuses or drops a start while a zone is running, chain the zones yourself. Open the second zone's automation, choose Take control from its menu (the automation stops following the blueprint and becomes editable), and replace its trigger: instead of the start event, trigger on the first controller zone turning off (a state trigger on that entity, from on to off). Keep the actions as they are. Do the same for the third zone on the second, and so on: the zones water in the order you chose, each for its own duration. The automations that keep the blueprint still update when the blueprint does; the ones you took control of do not, which is fine, they are two lines long.

docs.title: Rain Bird
docs.text:
• Controller zone entity: the zone's switch (one is created for every zone on the controller).
  • Turn off its schedule: in the Rain Bird app, disable each program, or remove every watering day from it. Do not put the controller's dial on OFF: on most models that blocks every run, including the ones started from the app or from Home Assistant.
  • The integration polls the controller once a minute, so the zone's state in Home Assistant can lag the valve by up to a minute. That matters only for observed watering, not for the blueprint.

docs.title: Hunter Hydrawise
docs.text:
• Controller zone entity: the zone's binary sensor that shows whether it is watering (device class running), not a switch. That is the entity the hydrawise.start_watering action targets, and the blueprint's list is filtered to it.
  • Turn off its schedule: every zone has an auto_watering switch in Home Assistant. Turning it off suspends the zone's Smart Watering schedule for a year (that is how the integration implements it), while runs started from Home Assistant still work. You can also suspend the zone in the Hydrawise app.

docs.title: Rachio
docs.text:
• Controller zone entity: the zone's switch.
  • Turn off its schedule: each Rachio schedule is a switch in Home Assistant, turn the ones that cover the zone off, or disable them in the Rachio app.
  • The 3 hour cap is Rachio's, see above.
  • Rachio updates Home Assistant through the cloud: the integration's page explains that your Home Assistant must be reachable from the internet for zone states to update. The blueprint does not depend on that (it waits the duration it asked for), observed watering does.
  • The integration's option "duration in minutes when activating a zone switch" is a failsafe for the switch. The blueprint passes its own duration to the action and does not use it.

docs.title: OpenSprinkler
docs.text:
• Controller zone entity: the station's enabled switch (the integration marks it with device class station; the blueprint's list is filtered to those). It is the entity the opensprinkler.run_station action takes, and the station must be enabled or the run is refused.
  • Turn off its schedule: each OpenSprinkler program has an enabled switch in Home Assistant, turn them off, or disable the programs in the OpenSprinkler interface. Keep the controller's own enabled switch on.
  • Runs are queued, so several zones asked at once water one after the other.
  • Up to beta 5 the blueprint called opensprinkler.run, which the integration has deprecated. It now calls opensprinkler.run_station. If you imported the blueprint before that, import it again.

docs.title: Orbit B-hyve
docs.text:
• Controller zone entity: the zone's valve entity (a switch on older versions of the integration).
  • Turn off its schedule: in Home Assistant, turn off the zone's smart watering switch and each program switch that includes the zone, or do the same in the B-hyve app.
  • The integration recommends bhyve.start_watering with a number of minutes over opening the valve, because some devices cannot set a default watering time. That is what the blueprint uses.

docs.title: Telling us how it went
docs.text: Each blueprint says in its description that it is not yet confirmed on real hardware. When you have run one, please post in the discussions: the controller model, whether the zone started and stopped at the right time, and anything you had to change. Once a controller is confirmed we remove the warning from its blueprint.

docs.title: Enhanced Scheduling and Executor Integration
docs.text: This document describes the enhanced scheduling capabilities and how Smart Irrigation hands its calculated run times to the schedulers and controllers that drive the valves: Irrigation Unlimited and Irrigation-V5.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Smart Irrigation includes recurring schedules and seasonal adjustments of its own, and hands its calculated run times to Irrigation Unlimited and Irrigation-V5 through blueprints and automations.

docs.title: Recurring Schedules
docs.text:
Recurring schedules are on their way out. They keep working until version 2027.11 at the earliest, and each call to create_recurring_schedule, update_recurring_schedule or delete_recurring_schedule raises a repair issue. The programs' schedules do the same and are in the panel, under Watering (full controller). See actions on their way out.

Create flexible recurring schedules that automatically trigger irrigation calculations, updates, or irrigation events.

docs.title: Schedule Types
docs.text:
1. Daily Schedules: Run every day at a specified time
  2. Weekly Schedules: Run on specific days of the week
  3. Monthly Schedules: Run on a specific day of each month
  4. Interval Schedules: Run every X hours

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Use the new services to create and manage recurring schedules:

service: smart_irrigation.create_recurring_schedule
data:
  name: "Morning Calculation"
  type: "daily"
  time: "06:00"
  action: "calculate"
  zones: "all"
  enabled: true

docs.title: Schedule Actions
docs.text:
• calculate: Trigger irrigation calculations for specified zones
  • update: Update weather data for specified zones
  • irrigate: Fire irrigation start event for specified zones

docs.title: Seasonal Adjustments
docs.text: Automatically adjust irrigation parameters based on the season or time of year.

docs.title: Adjustment Types
docs.text:
1. Multiplier Adjustments: Scale the crop factor of the zones, which scales the evapotranspiration (1 changes nothing)
  2. Threshold Adjustments: Adjust the irrigation threshold (water balance)

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
service: smart_irrigation.set_seasonal_adjustment
data:
  name: "Summer Boost"
  month_start: 6  # June
  month_end: 8    # August
  multiplier_adjustment: 1.5
  threshold_adjustment: -5.0
  zones: "all"
  enabled: true

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Smart Irrigation calculates how long each zone should water, and Irrigation Unlimited runs the valves. The two do not talk to each other directly: the duration is handed over by a blueprint or an automation that calls Irrigation Unlimited's own adjust_time action. There is nothing to enable in either integration, and no configuration.yaml block to add for Smart Irrigation, which is UI-only (adding one causes a setup error on restart).

docs.title: The sync services are gone
docs.text:
sync_with_irrigation_unlimited, send_zone_data_to_irrigation_unlimited and get_irrigation_unlimited_status have been removed. They belonged to a sync subsystem that was switched off and had no setting to switch it on: the flag it read was never a setting of this integration, so it could not work for anyone, and calling one returned quietly with a warning in the log. That cost at least one person an evening of looking for a mistake in their own configuration (discussion #696).

It also worked by guessing which Irrigation Unlimited entity belonged to which zone from their names, which is not something to build on.

Use the blueprint instead. It hands Irrigation Unlimited the calculated duration through IU's own adjust_time action and lets IU run the valves, which is the division of labour both integrations are built for.

docs.title: Using Both Integrations Together
docs.text:
1. Primary Controller: Choose either Smart Irrigation or Irrigation Unlimited as your primary controller
  2. Data Flow: Use Smart Irrigation for calculations and Irrigation Unlimited for execution
  3. Scheduling: Use Smart Irrigation's enhanced scheduling with Irrigation Unlimited's execution
  4. Monitoring: Monitor both systems for comprehensive irrigation oversight

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
1. Smart Irrigation: Calculate irrigation needs based on weather and ET
  2. Blueprint or automation: Hand the calculated durations to Irrigation Unlimited with adjust_time
  3. Irrigation Unlimited: Execute irrigation schedules with hardware control
  4. Feedback: Monitor execution and adjust parameters as needed

docs.title: Example Integration Automation
docs.text:
Irrigation Unlimited exposes binary_sensor entities (not switches). Use the irrigation_unlimited.adjust_time service to pass the calculated duration to IU, then let IU handle execution:

automation:
  - alias: "Smart Irrigation → IU: push duration for zone 1"
    trigger:
      - platform: time
        at: "23:00:00"
    condition:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ states('sensor.smart_irrigation_zone_1') | int(0) > 0 }}"
    action:
      - service: irrigation_unlimited.adjust_time
        data:
          entity_id: binary_sensor.irrigation_unlimited_c1_z1
          actual: "{{ timedelta(seconds=states('sensor.smart_irrigation_zone_1') | int(0)) }}"

The water balance reset can be handled by a separate automation that triggers when the IU zone turns off (see the Irrigation Unlimited reset water balance blueprint, which you can import in one click from the blueprints table).

docs.title: Irrigation-V5
docs.text:
Irrigation-V5 is another scheduler and controller. Like Irrigation Unlimited it does not calculate anything, so Smart Irrigation supplies the run time and V5 runs the valves.

No automation is needed for this one. V5 reads a numeric entity as a multiplier on a zone's watering time, and its author documents the trick that turns that into "run for exactly this many seconds":

  1. In the zone's advanced options, set the watering unit to seconds.
  2. Set the zone's watering time to 1.
  3. Set the zone's Adjustment Sensor to the Smart Irrigation sensor for that zone, sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name].

V5 then runs for 1 x the value of our sensor seconds, which is the calculated duration. When Smart Irrigation says no irrigation is needed the sensor reads 0, the multiplier is 0, and V5 skips the zone: the decision of whether to water and of how long both come from the calculation.

Keep the unit of our duration sensor as seconds. It has a duration device class, so Home Assistant lets you change the displayed unit per entity; switching it to minutes would make V5 read minutes as if they were seconds and water for a sixtieth of the time.

docs.title: Crediting the water balance with Irrigation-V5
docs.text:
V5 drives your own valve or solenoid entity, which means Smart Irrigation can simply watch that same entity: enable observed watering and set the zone's linked entity to the valve V5 operates (see closed loop). The water balance is then credited from the run that actually happened, and no reset automation is needed.

If you prefer to stay open loop, call smart_irrigation.set_bucket from your own automation when the valve turns off, and do not enable observed watering as well, or the water balance is credited twice.

docs.title: Automation Blueprints
docs.text: See the blueprints page for the full list and which one to pick, and the off-the-shelf controllers page for Rain Bird, Hydrawise, Rachio, OpenSprinkler and B-hyve. For Irrigation Unlimited, use the adjust time blueprint that matches your setup (a zone of its own, or a zone inside a sequence) together with the reset bucket one. Either way it is one automation per zone: a sequence adjusted as a whole spreads the time you give it across its zones in proportion to their original durations, so a calculated duration handed to the sequence would water every zone by the wrong amount.

docs.title: Enhanced Scheduling Services
docs.text:
• smart_irrigation.set_seasonal_adjustment: without adjustment_id it creates one, with it it changes that one, and with remove: true as well it removes it
  • smart_irrigation.create_recurring_schedule, update_recurring_schedule, delete_recurring_schedule: on their way out, see above

docs.title: Enhanced Scheduling Events
docs.text:
• smart_irrigation_recurring_schedule_triggered
  • smart_irrigation_seasonal_adjustment_applied

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. Schedules Not Running: Verify schedule configuration and enabled status
  2. Seasonal Adjustments Not Applied: Check month ranges and zone specifications
  3. Irrigation Unlimited Not Getting the Duration: Check that the blueprint or automation runs, and that its Irrigation Unlimited entity exists (a binary_sensor)

docs.title: Debug Logging
docs.text:
Enable debug logging for detailed information:

logger:
  logs:
    custom_components.smart_irrigation.scheduler: debug

docs.title: Backward Compatibility
docs.text: All enhanced features are optional and maintain full backward compatibility with existing Smart Irrigation installations.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
1. Existing installations continue to work without changes
  2. New features are opt-in through configuration or service calls
  3. Legacy automations remain functional

docs.title: Integration with Existing Setups
docs.text: The enhanced features complement existing Smart Irrigation functionality: - Existing triggers continue to work - Current automations remain functional - New features can be gradually adopted

docs.title: Basic Recurring Schedule
docs.text:
# Daily morning calculation
service: smart_irrigation.create_recurring_schedule
data:
  name: "Daily Morning Check"
  type: "daily" 
  time: "06:00"
  action: "calculate"
  zones: "all"

docs.title: Seasonal Adjustment
docs.text:
# Summer irrigation boost
service: smart_irrigation.set_seasonal_adjustment
data:
  name: "Summer Heat Adjustment"
  month_start: 6
  month_end: 8
  multiplier_adjustment: 1.3
  zones: "all"

This enhanced functionality provides Smart Irrigation users with professional-grade scheduling capabilities while maintaining the simplicity and reliability they expect.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
Each zone you configure will be added as a sensor entity to Home Assistant. The sensor will be named as follows: sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone_name]. So if you have a zone called 'lawn' then the sensor would be named sensor.smart_irrigation_lawn.

Each entity will have the following attributes:

Attribute Description id internal identification size the total area the irrigation system reaches in m2 or sq ft. throughput total amount of water that flows through the irrigation system in liters or gallon per minute. input_method how the precipitation rate is determined: throughput (from size + throughput) or direct (entered directly). precipitation_rate the directly entered precipitation rate in mm/h or in/h, when input_method is direct. state disabled, manual, automatic bucket the water balance, in mm or inch. The attribute keeps the name bucket, as do maximum_bucket and the entity ids ending in _bucket, so automations keep working. bucket_unit, size_unit, throughput_unit, drainage_rate_unit, current_drainage_unit, maximum_bucket_unit, precipitation_rate_unit, et_value_unit, et_deficiency_unit, eto_unit the unit each figure is shown in, following the unit system of Home Assistant (mm or inch, m2 or sq ft, liter or gallon per minute). multiplier the zone's crop factor (Kc). lead_time the lead time of the zone, in seconds. maximum_duration the maximum duration of a run for the zone, in seconds. drainage_rate how fast a saturated root zone drains, per hour (see drainage_rate_unit). current_drainage the water drained at the last calculation. maximum_bucket the most water the root zone holds above field capacity. last_updated when weather data was last retrieved for the zone. last_calculated when the zone was last calculated. number_of_data_points how many readings the last calculation worked from. et_value the net precipitation applied to the water balance by the last calculation, in mm or inch: the water need over the interval with the precipitation already subtracted from it. It is positive on a day where more rain fell than water evaporated. Despite its name this is not the evapotranspiration. et_deficiency what this zone needs, per day, before the interval scaling and before precipitation, in mm or inch. Negative, because it is what the soil lost. It carries the zone's crop factor, so it is ETc = ET0 x Kc and it agrees with the water balance beside it. Unlike the water balance it does not depend on the calculation interval or on water balance resets, so this is the value to compare when trying out configurations. eto the reference evapotranspiration of the same run, positive, with no crop factor. This is the number the literature and the weather services quote, so it is the one to hold against an external ET0 figure. unit_of_measurement seconds device_class duration icon default: mdi:sprinkler friendly_name Name of your zone.

Sample screenshot:

If you want to expose these attributes as separate sensors, you can add template sensors using a template like the following example for bucket:

{{state_attr('sensor.smart_irrigation_your_zone_sensor_name', 'bucket')}}

(Since the per-zone device was added, you can also just use the dedicated entities below instead of template sensors.)

docs.title: Per-zone device and entities
docs.text:
Each zone is also grouped as a device in Home Assistant (named after the zone), attached to the single Smart Irrigation hub device. Alongside the duration sensor above, the device exposes dedicated entities, so a zone reads as a set of entities rather than one attribute bag:

Entity Type Description Duration (sensor.smart_irrigation_[zone]) sensor Calculated watering duration (seconds). This is the original entity: its entity_id, recorded history and attributes are preserved. Water balance sensor Current soil water balance (mm/inch); negative means deficit. This is the value the last calculation committed. Live water balance sensor Where the zone stands now: the same calculation run over the readings collected since the last one, without committing anything. Recomputed as the zone's readings arrive, at most every thirty seconds. Its live attribute is false when there is nothing to estimate from yet (just after a calculation), and the value is then the committed water balance; since, as_of and duration say what the estimate covers and the run it implies. Applied ET sensor The same figure as the et_value attribute: the net precipitation applied to the water balance at the last calculation (the water need over the interval, et0 x interval, with the rain already subtracted). Positive when more rain fell than water evaporated. Despite its name it is not the evapotranspiration; for that see Daily ET deficiency and the eto attribute. Diagnostic, disabled on a new zone. Daily ET deficiency sensor This zone's daily need, crop factor included, independent of the interval and of rain. The et_deficiency attribute of the duration sensor. Diagnostic, disabled on a new zone. Current drainage sensor Water drained as runoff at the last calculation. The current_drainage attribute of the duration sensor. Diagnostic, disabled on a new zone. Last irrigation sensor (timestamp) When the zone was last credited for a run. Water used sensor (water, total) Cumulative water delivered to the zone (litres). Multiplier number Editable per-zone crop factor, written to the store and used by the next calculation. Listed under Configuration. Irrigation needed binary_sensor On when the water balance is in deficit. Watering now binary_sensor On while the zone's linked valve/switch is open. Problem binary_sensor On when a valve problem was reported (e.g. it never opened); clears on the next successful run. Calculate button Recalculate this zone now. Reset water balance button Set the water balance to 0 ("I just watered, start from zero"). Reset usage button Zero the cumulative water-used counter. Irrigate now button Run this zone's valve for its calculated duration (only shown with Calculate and water). The run credits the water balance, so the delivered water is accounted for and the next calculation irrigates less. The zone (valve.smart_irrigation_[zone]) valve The zone as a water valve, for dashboards, voice assistants and valve.open_valve / valve.close_valve. Open waters the zone for its calculated duration, like Irrigate now and water_zone: behind a run in progress it takes its turn, and the run credits the water balance. Close stops the zone's watering, and closes its valve when something else had opened it. It shows open or closed as the linked valve does. Available with Calculate and water when the zone has a linked valve.

Diagnostic, Configuration, disabled. Applied ET, Daily ET deficiency and Current drainage repeat an attribute of the duration sensor that few dashboards show, so they are diagnostic entities and a zone created since 2026.11 has them disabled: enable one in its entity settings when you want it. A zone that already had them keeps them as they were. The Multiplier is a setting and is listed under Configuration, as are the hub's Skip on precipitation and Precipitation threshold. Home Assistant leaves diagnostic and configuration entities out of the dashboards it generates; a dashboard of your own can show them like any other.

The Smart Irrigation hub device also carries global action buttons: calculate all zones, refresh weather, and (with Calculate and water) irrigate all zones. It has the master switch, Calculate and water (switch.smart_irrigation_irrigation_enabled): off, nothing is calculated and nothing is watered (see Stop everything; with Calculate only it stays on, see Calculate and water, calculate only, or stop everything). It also has a switch, Skip on precipitation, and a number, Precipitation threshold, both under Configuration: the rain forecast skip of the Skip watering page, which you can change from an automation or a dashboard. The number is in mm, or inch with the imperial unit system.

Postponing from a dashboard. The hub device also has two buttons, Postpone watering 24 h and Postpone watering 48 h, a Resume watering button, and a datetime entity, Watering postponed until (datetime.smart_irrigation_postponed_until). The datetime shows the end of the postponement in force, or nothing, and setting it holds the watering back until that moment: a date and time for the end of your holidays, for instance, from a dashboard or an automation. A moment already past lifts the postponement. They all do what the postpone_irrigation and resume_irrigation services do, and what the Postpone buttons of the Info page do.

docs.title: Program sensors
docs.text:
With the full controller on, each program has one sensor on the hub device: sensor.smart_irrigation_program_<id>, named "Program ". A program that is added gets its sensor, and one that is deleted loses it. The state is one of idle, waiting, running, paused or suspended. The attributes: Attribute Description program_id the id of the program, which is also in the entity id. next_start the next time a schedule starts it, or empty. last_run when it last started. suspended_until the end of its suspension, or empty. adjustment the adjust_program adjustment in force (percent, seconds and until), or empty. manual while it waits or runs: true when it was asked for by hand rather than by a schedule. tour, tours while it runs: the round it is on and how many rounds it has (both count from 1; tour is 0 while it waits). step, steps while it runs: the step it is on and how many steps the round has (step is 0 while it waits). percent while it runs: how far along it is, 0 to 100. remaining_seconds while it runs: the time left, paused time excluded.

The attributes from manual down are only there while the program waits or runs.

A program has no on and off switch of its own: it starts on its own through its schedules that are on. To keep one from watering (say, for the holidays), switch its schedules off with set_schedule_enabled, or suspend it. The program switch entities of 2026.11.0 are gone; the migration switched off the schedules of a program that was off.

These entities are additive: nothing was removed. The duration sensor keeps its entity_id, recorded history and attributes, so existing dashboards, automations and templates keep working. A one-time registry migration moves the duration sensor's internal unique_id to a stable per-zone scheme; the entity_id and history carry over.

The per-zone device/entity layout is inspired by JustChr's Smart Irrigation fork (MIT).

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
After installation, the following events are available:

Event Description smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones Fired when an irrigation start trigger is reached, or, with the full controller, when a schedule of the program that was the main one (id main) is due (trigger_type is then program). Listen to it to start your irrigation. See automations for examples. smart_irrigation_leak Fired when a zone's meter counts water with every valve closed, with Leak alert after set. Data: flow_sensor, litres, zone_ids, zones. smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped Fired when a start trigger is reached and the day is a skip day, so nothing is watered. Data: the trigger's identity, plus reason and checks, the same detail the Home page shows. The reason is the skip condition that held the day back: postponed, rain_sensor, freeze, wind, precipitation, days_between or soil_moisture. A trigger reached while Smart Irrigation is stopped fires it with the reason irrigation_off, and while it calculates only with the reason calculate_only (and no checks).

When Smart Irrigation waters, it fires three more, described in closed-loop irrigation. The full controller adds its own, with the data of each described there: program_started, program_finished, valve_on, valve_off, valve_out_of_sync and supply_problem. These three are also fired:

Event Description smart_irrigation_zone_unwatered A zone has been dry for more than 3 days and no program will water it; fired once per zone, together with a repair notice. Data: zone_id, zone, days, deficit_mm. See the dry zone notice. smart_irrigation_weather_stale A temperature, humidity, dew point, wind speed or pressure source of a sensor group has not reported for 6 hours; fired once per silence. Data: mapping_id, mapping, fields (the fields that just went silent) and since (the time of the last report). smart_irrigation_weather_recovered Fields that were silent report again, or the outage stops being watched. Data: mapping_id, mapping, fields, and reason when it is not a recovery: unloaded (the integration was reloaded, disabled or removed) or unwatched (no automatic zone uses the group any more).

Only zone_unwatered needs the full controller; weather_stale and weather_recovered do not.

docs.title: Knowing a run was skipped
docs.text:
A skipped day used to be the absence of an event, and nothing can listen for something that does not happen. That is why the skip now fires its own event:

automation:
  - alias: "Tell me when irrigation was skipped"
    trigger:
      - platform: event
        event_type: smart_irrigation_irrigation_skipped
    action:
      - service: notify.persistent_notification
        data:
          message: "No irrigation today: {{ trigger.event.data.reason }}"

The Home page answers the same question without an automation: it shows whether the next start would be skipped and why, and what the last real decision was.

docs.title: When does it fire?
docs.text:
The event fires when the active start trigger is reached. You can define several triggers, but only the one selected as active starts the watering, so the run happens once per day. The Start triggers card on the General page has the choice:

  • A trigger you defined. A solar event (sunrise, sunset or solar azimuth), optionally shifted by an offset, or a fixed clock time. A fixed time suits irrigation that has to be done by a certain hour whatever the season, rather than following the sun.
  • Default. Used whenever Default is selected, even if you have defined triggers. It starts early enough before sunrise that watering finishes at sunrise: sunrise minus the planned length of the run. That length is how long the run really takes, so with zones in parallel it is the longest zone rather than the sum, and the soak and pauses between zones are counted when Smart Irrigation opens the valves itself.
  • None. Nothing starts the watering, whatever the weather. The durations are still calculated. It is the way to keep Smart Irrigation from starting a run.

With account for duration on, a trigger works back from its moment so watering finishes then; with it off, watering starts then. That applies to a fixed time as well: set 06:30 with it on and an hour-long run starts at 05:30.

The skip conditions still apply: on a skip day no start event is fired, and the skipped event above is fired instead.

docs.title: Event data
docs.text:
The event carries the identity of the trigger that fired, so a single automation can react differently per trigger:

field meaning trigger_name the name you gave the trigger trigger_type sunrise, sunset, solar_azimuth or time. With the full controller, a start or a skip decided for a program's schedule has program, and carries program_id and schedule_id too at for a time trigger, the clock time it is set to offset_minutes the configured offset, in minutes account_for_duration whether timing is shifted so watering finishes at the target moment

Example: filter on trigger_name to react to a specific trigger.

trigger:
  - platform: event
    event_type: smart_irrigation_start_irrigation_all_zones
    event_data:
      trigger_name: "Morning"

docs.title: Coming from Irrigation Unlimited
docs.text:
Irrigation Unlimited (IU) is a scheduler and a sequencer of valves with no water model: it does not know the weather, the evapotranspiration or how much water a zone has lost. Smart Irrigation does, and until now the two were joined by two automations written by hand (adjust_time into IU, reset_bucket at the end).

The full controller does the scheduling and the running itself. This page says where each thing you used in IU went. It can also bring your configuration over for you: see Importing your configuration.

docs.title: The words
docs.text: In Irrigation Unlimited In Smart Irrigation Controller (and its master entity) Supply: a pump or a main valve, with a delay before and after that can be negative Zone Zone, with its linked valve (and, if it needs several, other valves) Sequence Program Sequence zone (a step) Step: one zone, or several watered together Step with zones in parallel A step with several zones, watered at the same time Delay between steps, including a negative one Wait after this step; a negative value overlaps the steps (up to an hour) adjust_time (actual, percentage, increase, decrease) The step's duration: calculated (the default), calculated times a percentage, or fixed, with a minimum, a maximum (min_seconds, max_seconds) and an offset in seconds (adjust_seconds: -120, YAML only, see YAML-only options). For a temporary change of a whole program, smart_irrigation.adjust_program (a percent and/or seconds, for some hours or until reset). You no longer need an automation to hand it the duration, because the calculated one is the default. reset_bucket or set_bucket after the run Nothing to do: a run of ours credits the water balance itself, for the water that went through suspend smart_irrigation.suspend, for a zone or a program, for some hours or until a date manual_run smart_irrigation.water_zone or smart_irrigation.run_program. A manual run joins the queue and takes its turn by default (mode: queue); mode: replace stops what is running first. run_program also takes seconds, a total shared between the steps, and stop_program ends one program. cancel smart_irrigation.stop_watering Pause and resume smart_irrigation.pause_watering and resume_watering Skip to the next step smart_irrigation.next_step Schedule (time, sun, cron) A program's schedules: time of day or sun (with an offset, and a fallback time for polar days, fallback_time: previous, YAML only, see YAML-only options), with the days as filters. Cron is not supported as such; the import turns a cron line with a bounded set of times into time schedules. anchor: start and anchor: finish The schedule's moment is when the program starts, or when it must be done (the start is worked back from the length of the run) Weekdays, day of the month, even/odd, every_n_days, months, from/to The same filters, on each schedule: days of the week, every N days, and a period of the year that may span New Year, in the form; the shift of every N days (every_offset: 1), even or odd days (parity: even), named days of the month (days_of_month: [1, 15, last]) and months (months: [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]) are YAML only, see YAML-only options entity_states Not the same feature. In IU it lets a timed valve receive only the on command, only the off, or neither. We have no such switch. The nearest things are the per-zone safety off mode (auto, zha, off), which can arm a hardware timed off (MQTT topic, or a ZHA command) as a dead-man behind the normal close, and the check while a valve is open. The ZHA timed off is armed automatically for a Sonoff SWV (tested on a real valve, ZHA, firmware 1.0.04: it honours the command and counts the time in seconds); for any other ZHA model it is opt-in (zha mode) because the unit of the time is unverified. A Sonoff SWV in auto mode is now also opened by that timed command, so it never runs without its own timer. See closed loop. check_back (delay, retries) The zone's Wait for the valve to confirm and Send the open again (open_resends, YAML only: the zone's Edit in YAML); the wait is in its advanced settings. The wait applies to the open and the close. A valve that closes by itself while it should be open is caught by the check every 60 seconds and is not reopened (see sync_error below) irrigation_unlimited_start and finish events smart_irrigation_program_started and program_finished valve_on and valve_off events smart_irrigation_valve_on and valve_off, for zones and supplies sync_error smart_irrigation_valve_out_of_sync, with a smart_irrigation_zone_problem of reason valve_closed_early: a valve held open that reads closed switch_error smart_irrigation_zone_problem (a zone valve) and supply_problem (a pump or main valve)

docs.title: What is different
docs.text:
• Programs never overlap. IU lets overlapping runs go on together; here a second program waits for the first, and a step with several zones (or a negative wait between steps) is how you ask for zones at the same time. A pump on a home network seldom has the pressure for more.
  • The weather is part of the schedule. A schedule skips, shortens or holds back what the skip conditions say. Turn it off per schedule if you want a plain timer.
  • The default duration is the one Smart Irrigation calculated, not a number you type.
  • Nothing is configured in YAML. It is all in the panel, and a restart goes on with the steps still to do instead of dropping a run that was under way.

docs.title: Importing your configuration
docs.text:
In Settings, General, the card Import from Irrigation Unlimited opens a wizard that reads your IU configuration and turns it into zones, programs, their schedules and supplies. It takes the configuration from where IU has it: your YAML (configuration.yaml and its includes, as Home Assistant loaded it), IU's own settings when it was set up in the interface, or YAML you paste. Pasted YAML is read as text: !include, !secret and !env_var are not followed, and the report says so.

Nothing is changed before you have seen it all:

  1. Zones: each IU zone is matched to one of your zones (by the one you choose, then by its valve, the blueprint that feeds it, or its name) or created. A zone you already have keeps its settings and only gets the fields it had empty.
  2. Programs and supplies: what each IU sequence and controller becomes, step by step. A sequence fed by Smart Irrigation's durations (an adjust-time automation) waters the calculated duration; the others keep IU's fixed times. The automation may adjust the sequence (with its zones) or each zone's own entity (binary_sensor.irrigation_unlimited_c1_z1, …): IU applies a zone's adjustment inside every sequence that waters it, so a step whose zones are all fed that way is calculated too.
  3. The report: what was carried over exactly, what was approximated (a cron expression turned into times, for example) and what has no equivalent here.

The schedules of new programs are created switched off, so IU keeps watering until you are ready to switch over. The wizard says so differently when IU is not running, for instance because Home Assistant rejected its configuration: nothing waters then until you switch the schedules on.

Switching the full controller on, which the programs need, creates a program with every zone that has a valve when there is no program yet. If you import first, the imported programs are the ones that water: a program only waters the zones of its steps. A program of your own that waters the same zones as the imported ones waters them twice: switch its schedules off under Programs. Importing again later updates what the earlier import made, in place, and removes what IU no longer has; the wizard asks before it removes anything. Only an administrator can import.

docs.title: Switching over
docs.text:
At the top of the import page, once something is imported:

  • Switch over to Smart Irrigation switches off IU's controllers that are on (irrigation_unlimited.disable, which IU keeps across a restart), then switches on the imported schedules that IU had on. A sequence or zone schedule that IU runs switched off, or whose controller is off, stays off here too. A zone that IU runs switched off inside a sequence is named on the page: IU leaves it out, but here its step waters it until you switch that step off. If the import has no record of which schedules IU had on (an import from before this was kept), none of that program's schedules comes on and the page says so: switch them on yourself, or go back, import again and switch over again. IU is switched off first, so for a moment nothing waters rather than both.
  • Go back to Irrigation Unlimited switches the imported schedules off first, then on again the controllers the switch turned off, and no others. Which schedules were on is kept: switching over again brings back those, including your own changes.
  • If a step fails, the one before it is undone, and the page says who waters.
  • Who waters is read from what is on, not from the buttons: if IU switches a controller on again (by hand, or because IU does not restore its state) while imported schedules are on, or you switch a schedule on by hand while IU waters, the page says that both would water and offers to switch IU off. It also says when nothing waters.
  • What still uses Irrigation Unlimited lists your automations and scripts that name IU's services, events (irrigation_unlimited_start, _finish, …) or entities, with a link to each. An adjust-time automation has nothing left to do: the steps are calculated here. Nothing is changed for you.

After the switch, importing again keeps the on or off you gave each schedule, and a schedule new to the import comes with IU's own on and off, since IU no longer waters.

docs.title: What the import does not carry over
docs.text:
• A controller with a master becomes a supply, and its programs water beside the other controllers', as in IU. Controllers without a master share the mains: their programs run one after the other.
  • Runs that IU overlapped run one after the other.
  • A step's repeat becomes passes: the water in parts with a soak between, not full runs.
  • entity_states, threshold, a zone's default duration for manual runs, the master's check_back and volume, an unbounded cron, a sun event other than sunrise and sunset.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
If you would rather rebuild than import:

  1. Switch on the full controller.
  2. Add your pump or main valve as a supply, and pick it in each zone.
  3. Make a program per IU sequence: its steps are the sequence's zones, in order. Leave the duration on calculated.
  4. Add a schedule to each. If IU ran it to finish at sunrise, take Sunrise, must be done.
  5. Switch IU's own schedules off, and remove the two automations that handed it durations and reset the water balance.
  6. Look at the Planning card: it shows the next days (3, 7 or 14, as you pick on the chart). Compare it with what IU would have done before you remove IU.

docs.title: Not in Smart Irrigation
docs.text:
• Cron schedules (the import expands a bounded one into time schedules).
  • Several independent controllers, each with its own sequences. Several supplies are possible, and each zone picks its own, but there is one program queue.
  • Overlap of whole programs: only the steps of one program can overlap (negative wait), never two programs.
  • An adjustable granularity, renaming the entities IU creates, a built-in simulator.
  • IU's entity_states choice of which commands a timed valve receives.

docs.title: Not in Irrigation Unlimited
docs.text:
• A water model: evapotranspiration, a water balance per zone, and a water balance credit for the water that really went through.
  • Durations calculated from the weather, instead of typed.
  • Weather skip conditions (rain, frost, wind, wet soil) that can be set per schedule.
  • Hardware dead-man arming (MQTT or ZHA) and a check that a valve did not close by itself while it should be open.

docs.title: Full controller
docs.text:
By default Smart Irrigation decides how long each zone waters and leaves the running of the valves to you: an automation, a controller, Irrigation Unlimited. The full controller is an option for those who would rather have it do both. It runs the whole watering itself: when, in what order, with which pump, for how long, and what to do when you want it to stop.

It is off by default, and turning it on changes nothing until you add to it. Nothing on this page appears in the panel until it is on.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
The full controller is what Calculate and water means: choose it in Settings, General, in the first card's list, What Smart Irrigation does. There is no other switch to turn on.

Choosing it:

  • lets Smart Irrigation open and close the valves itself, and turns on observed watering, so a watering by hand counts too;
  • waters with programs, each one the zones of its steps, started by its own schedules. When there is no program yet, it creates one with the zones that have a valve and a schedule that starts it as your start trigger did (done by sunrise by default), so nothing changes in when you water. A zone added later is watered once a program has it in a step: the setup assistant puts a new zone in one for you;
  • adds a Watering tab to the panel, with three pages: Planning, Programs and Pumps. The cards below are in it.

Choosing Calculate only goes back to calculating for an automation of your own: Smart Irrigation fires its start event at the start trigger and opens no valve. Your programs and supplies stay stored for the day you choose Calculate and water again.

Up to 2026.11.0 this took two switches, Full controller and Let Smart Irrigation control the valve, and the main program of that time could also be started by the start trigger or switched off on its own. An installation is moved over once, keeping its watering as it was: direct valve control alone becomes Calculate and water, the active start trigger becomes a schedule of the program that was the main program, now an ordinary program called Watering (see below; the other triggers you had defined become schedules switched off, so none is lost: switch one on to use it), and if it was switched off its schedules stay switched off.

No main program any more (2026.11.1). Up to 2026.11.0 a special main program watered every zone with a valve, in the order of the general settings, and the other programs had steps. Now every program is the same kind. Your main program was turned once into an ordinary program, so it waters exactly as before: it keeps its id main (its sensor, its last runs and its notifications stay) and its schedules, and its name unless it was still the default Main program, which becomes Watering in the language of Home Assistant (a name you changed is kept); and gets explicit steps, the zones it watered in the same order. With one after the other, one step per zone, each followed by the pause between zones as its wait (none after the last); with all at once, one step with all the zones. Each step takes the calculated duration, in the passes the old setting asked for. A zone added afterwards is not watered until a program has it in a step. The Program on setting and its switch entity are gone too: a program starts on its own through the schedules that are on, so a program that was off had its schedules switched off. Run now always works. The set_program_enabled action is deprecated and will be removed in 2027.11: it still works, switching all of a program's schedules on or off, and raises a repair notice; use set_schedule_enabled instead.

One thing is different from the moment it is on: a valve found open at startup that no run of ours owns is closed. After a crash or a restart, a valve left open by a run nobody resumes would water until someone noticed. A reading that says nothing (unavailable, unknown) is never taken for an open valve. That startup alignment also closes a zone's extra valves, and it looks at the supplies: a pump or main valve that is on while nothing holds it is switched off, and one whose state cannot be read yet is looked at again 30 and 120 seconds later, since its entity often comes up after Home Assistant has started.

docs.title: Pumps and main valves (supplies)
docs.text:
A supply is one or several entities, a pump or a main valve in front of the zone valves, that run while a zone they feed is being watered. Add them in the card Pumps and main valves, then pick one in each zone's settings.

Each supply has two delays, in seconds, and both are signed, from -3600 to +3600:

Positive Negative Delay before The supply comes on that long before the zone valve opens. The valve opens first, and the supply comes on that long after. Delay after The supply stays on that long after the zone valve closes. The supply goes off that long before the valve closes, so a pump never pushes against a closed valve.

Power cut before starting (kick_seconds, 0 to 60, 0 by default; advanced mode, and shown in every mode once it is not 0): for a pump whose pressure controller only starts again after its power has been cut, the supply is switched off that many seconds and then on, each time it is switched on. A supply already on for another zone is not cut again.

A supply is on while anything holds it, and goes off when the last hold is given back, after its delay. It is never switched off on a guess of when the cycle will end. Two zones in a row share one run of the pump, and with a delay after the pump stays on between them.

A supply that will not come on keeps the zone shut. Each switch call is tried twice, 3 seconds apart, and the entity must then read a state within 5 seconds. If the supply still has not come on, the zone's valve is not opened (no pump, no water), the run of that zone ends with a smart_irrigation_zone_problem of reason supply_did_not_turn_on, and smart_irrigation_supply_problem is fired too. A supply that will not go off never blocks anything: the off is tried again after 15, 45 and 120 seconds, smart_irrigation_supply_problem (reason supply_did_not_turn_off) is fired for the first failure (the retries are silent), and a supply still on after that stays recorded as on, so the next run or the next startup puts it off. The payload of supply_problem is supply_id, supply, entity_id and reason (supply_did_not_turn_on or supply_did_not_turn_off).

A zone can also have other valves that open and close with its own (a zone whose water comes through two valves), and light and cover entities are accepted as valves.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text:
A program is an ordered list of steps. A step is one zone, or several zones watered at the same time. By default a step takes the duration Smart Irrigation calculated for each zone, which is what sets this apart from a timer.

For each step:

  • Duration: calculated by Smart Irrigation (the default), calculated times a percentage (110 % in a heat wave, 50 % for a plant that needs less), or fixed (seconds of water). The lead time that fills the pipe is kept in every mode. A zone that needs no water gets none, unless the step is fixed.
  • Only water when the deficit is at least (min_deficit_mm, 0 to 100, 0 means none; YAML only, for instance min_deficit_mm: 7 on the step, see YAML-only options): a zone is only watered by the step when its water deficit (how far its water balance is below zero, in mm) is at least this. A zone under it sits the step out; this is only written in the log (reason below_deficit), not exposed anywhere else. It applies to calculated and percent steps; a fixed step is always watered. Set, it replaces the zone's own irrigation threshold for this step: a zone whose threshold of 20 mm has not been reached yet, at a deficit of 15 mm, is still watered by a step asking for 7 mm, for the run its water balance implies.
  • Minimum water, Maximum water and Time added (+) or removed (-) (min_seconds, max_seconds, adjust_seconds): the water of a step is raised to the minimum or capped at the maximum (0 means none, at most 86400 seconds each), and the time added or removed is a signed number of seconds (-6 h to +6 h). The time added or removed (adjust_seconds) is YAML only, for instance adjust_seconds: -120 on the step (see YAML-only options). A minimum never turns a zone that needs no water into watering: a calculated duration of zero stays zero. The lead time is added on top of these bounds. The order is below.
  • Fixed seconds (seconds, for a fixed step): at most 86400.
  • Percentage (for a percent step): 0 to 1000.
  • Water in several passes: the step's water is split into this many passes, 1 to 6, each zone soaking between two of them for the soak time, one setting for every program, shown next to the step's passes (cycle and soak).
  • Wait after this step: seconds before the next step, from -3600 to +21600. Empty is no wait. A negative wait overlaps the steps: the next one starts that many seconds before this one ends, so the valves and the pump of both are open together for that time (up to an hour, and never longer than this step runs).
  • Volume limit: a zone stops once its water meter has counted this many litres, at most 100000. The meter reports every so often, so it is not exact. A zone without a meter ignores it.

For the program:

  • Rounds (tours, YAML only, for instance tours: 2 at the top of the program, see YAML-only options): the whole list is watered this many times (1 to 6), each round with its share of the water. Unlike passes, which repeat a step before going on, a round waters every step once and starts again, so each zone soaks while the others water and no soak time is needed.

Any program can be deleted, the one with the id main included, except the last one: the panel shows no Delete button then, and a save that would leave no program is refused. To stop it watering, switch its schedules off.

How the duration of a step is worked out, in this order: the step's percentage (percent steps), then the percentage of an adjust_program adjustment in force, then the step's time added or removed plus the seconds of that adjustment, then the minimum, then the maximum (so when the minimum is larger than the maximum, the maximum wins). Nothing under zero is watered. These bounds apply to the total water of the step, before it is split across the rounds; the lead time comes on top of each pass.

One queue per supply. Programs whose zones share a supply take turns: a different program asked for while one runs waits its turn, and a manual run asked for during a program is added behind it. Zones without a supply share one queue, the mains, so an installation without supplies runs one program at a time. A program on the well pump and one on the mains share nothing and water side by side. A program waits for every supply its steps name (all of its zones, not only those the plan will water), and the runs that asked first go first on every supply, so one that needs two supplies is not overtaken by runs that need one. A one-off run of every zone waits for everything else, and everything else waits for it. A zone watered by hand (water_zone) waits only for its own supply. Pause, resume and Stop act on every run; Next step moves every program on, or one with program_id. A program that is already running or waiting is not queued a second time: run_program on it is ignored (with a line in the log), and so is a schedule that comes due meanwhile. The plan is worked out when the turn comes, from the zones as they are then: a zone watered meanwhile is not watered again.

docs.title: Seeing a program before it runs
docs.text: An unfolded program shows what a run would do: one line per zone on a time axis, its passes as bars, the time its pipe fills in a lighter shade and the soak between two passes hatched. Two zones of one step run side by side, a negative wait shows the next step starting before the last one ends, and the total is at the end of the axis. The durations are the ones Smart Irrigation would water now; they follow the weather, so a run may differ when it starts. The Planning page draws each run it lists, on the clock.

docs.title: A program in YAML
docs.text:
Edit in YAML shows the program as text, in place of the form, and back: a program written in YAML is an ordinary program once applied, and the form edits it as any other. To paste a program written elsewhere, add a New program and open it in YAML. Nothing is saved until Apply: as you type, the program is cleaned the way a save cleans it and drawn on the timeline, and a zone that does not exist, or one the run leaves out (no valve, or disabled), is named. Only a valid program can be applied.

The text is short on purpose, so it can be read, copied between installations or written by an assistant:

name: Evening
steps:
  - zones: [Vegetable garden, Greenhouse]   # watered together
    mode: percent
    percent: 80
    passes: 2
  - zones: [Hedges]
    delay: -60                              # the next step starts a minute early
schedules:
  - time: "21:00"
    weekdays: [0, 2, 4]                     # 0 is Monday

A step names its zones by name (case aside) or by number; a name two zones share is not guessed, use the number. What is left out takes its default, the same as the form: a calculated duration, one pass, no wait, a schedule that starts at its moment every day with the weather taken into account. The keys are the ones described above: for a step zones, mode (calculated, percent or fixed), percent, seconds, passes, delay, max_litres, min_seconds, max_seconds, adjust_seconds, min_deficit_mm and enabled; for the program name, tours, steps, schedules and notify (see below); for a schedule type (time, sun or after), time, event (sunrise, sunset or azimuth, with azimuth in degrees), after_program (with type: after: the program it starts after, by name or id; see Chaining programs), offset_minutes (0 or more with type: after), anchor (start or end), weekdays, every_n_days, every_offset, parity, days_of_month, months, from_date, until_date, weather, skip_conditions, hard_deadline and fallback_time. The id lines keep a program, a step or a schedule the same one across an edit (a schedule remembers its last run under its id): keep them when you edit, leave them out of a new program. An assistant can write and check a program for you: see Assistants (AI).

YAML-only options. As in Home Assistant's own visual editors, some options have no field in the form, even when they are set: they are written here, in YAML (or by the services or an assistant). Editing the program in the form keeps them as they are, and an unfolded program that uses one says so at its top, in a Set in YAML (not editable here) box listing them, with Edit in YAML at hand to change them. They are:

  • for the program: tours: 2, the rounds;
  • for a step: adjust_seconds: -120, the time added or removed, and min_deficit_mm: 7, only water when the deficit is at least;
  • for a schedule: every_offset: 1, the shift of every N days, parity: even (or odd), days_of_month: [1, 15, last] and months: [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], the days; fallback_time: previous (or "06:00"), for polar day and night; skip_conditions: [rain_sensor, freeze], only some of the checks (the Take the weather into account switch itself stays in the form).
  • for a zone, in its own Edit in YAML: safety_off_state_key: state_l1, the safety off state key, and open_resends: 0, how often the open is sent again.

docs.title: Being told when a program has watered
docs.text:
Each program has a Notifications section: tick whom to tell, and a summary is sent when the program has watered, one line per zone (minutes and, with a flow meter, litres) and one per problem (a valve that did not open, a run where no water flowed...). The targets are:

  • Notification in Home Assistant: a persistent notification, replaced by the next run of the same program;
  • the notify entities of Home Assistant;
  • the notify actions that are not an entity, such as notify.mobile_app_<phone> of the companion app. On a phone, a run that went wrong comes through with a high priority (Android) and as time-sensitive (iOS), and each program replaces its own previous notification.

When to tell: at the start and at the end of each watering (the start lists the zones about to be watered), only at the end, or only when something goes wrong. A valve that does not close and a pump or main valve that does not do what it is told are told at once, to the program under way, without waiting for the end of the run.

It is off until a target is ticked, and it changes nothing to a run. The events (smart_irrigation_program_finished, smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished...) are still fired, so an automation of your own keeps working beside it. In YAML:

notify:
  targets: [notify.mobile_app_pixel, persistent_notification]
  when: problems        # or finish
  start: false

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A program has any number of schedules, each a moment and the days it applies to.

  • The moment is a time of day, sunrise, sunset, or the moment the sun reaches a bearing (azimuth, in degrees clockwise from north: 90 east, 180 south, 270 west, for a bed the shade of a wall leaves at that moment), with minutes before (-) or after (+). It is either when the program starts or when it must be done. With the second, the start is worked back from the length of what the program has to water (its steps, waits, passes and soaks). A start that has gone by while its moment is still ahead begins at once rather than losing the day, but only after a restart or a reload of Home Assistant, or when its timer was missed. Editing a program, or a calculation that makes the run longer, never starts a run on the spot: an edit at 05:50 of a "done by 06:00" schedule that now needs 20 minutes waits for tomorrow. The same goes for a schedule that starts at its moment: if Home Assistant was down then, the run is caught up after the restart when it is at most 2 hours late and has not run for that occurrence; later than that, it is passed over to the next occurrence.
  • Cut the run at the end time (hard_deadline, only for a schedule that must be done by its moment): by default that moment is a target, and a run that starts late, or has a longer plan than expected, or is paused, simply ends later. Turn it on and the moment is a limit: at that time the zones still open are closed the normal way (each is credited for the water it delivered), the steps not started are dropped, and the program_finished event carries cut: true and reason: "deadline" (the log says so too). A run that gets its turn after the deadline has passed opens nothing. With a deadline, the zones of each step are also ordered driest first (lowest water balance, the largest water deficit); steps keep their order and the zones of a step still open together, so the ordering only decides which zone opens first. If the controller restarts mid-run, the deadline is kept with the run.
  • After a program (type: after): the schedule has no moment of its own and starts its program once another one has finished. See Chaining programs.
  • Polar day and night: a sunrise or sunset schedule has no moment on a day when the sun does not rise or set, and that day is skipped. If there is no sunrise or sunset (fallback_time) chooses what that day does: skip it (the default), use the time of the last sunrise or sunset seen (offset included, looking back at most 60 days; previous), or start at a fixed time (HH:MM). It is YAML only (or set by the services), for instance fallback_time: previous or fallback_time: "06:00" on the schedule (see YAML-only options).
  • Before or after the sun is limited to 12 hours either way (-720 to +720 minutes).
  • The days are filters, and all of them have to hold: they apply to the day of the moment. A run that must be done by Monday 01:00 and takes two hours starts on Sunday at 23:00, and "Monday" is the day that counts. The weather, on the other hand, is judged when the run starts, so that run asks Sunday's conditions. The filters are: days of the week; every N days (N up to 60) with a shift from 0 to N - 1 (three programs with N = 3 and shifts 0, 1 and 2 take turns and never share a day); even or odd days of the month; named days of the month (1, 15, last, where a month too short for a day skips it, 31 in April, and last is every month's own last day); months; and a period of the year, a month and a day picked for each end, which may run over New Year (from November to March; MM-DD in the service, 11-01 to 03-01). The panel's More options of a schedule has the days of the week, every N days and the period. The others are YAML only (or set by the services; see YAML-only options): the shift of every N days (every_offset: 1), even or odd days (parity: even or parity: odd), the days of the month (days_of_month: [1, 15, last]) and the months (months: [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], January is 1).
  • Take the weather into account (weather), a switch, on by default. On, the checks of Weather > Skip watering apply (rain, frost, wind, the days between irrigation, a wet soil, postponed days), with the same decision made once a day; on a day when rain is forecast, only the zones the rain cannot reach run. Off is for a greenhouse drip line that does not care (weather: false). In the drawing of a program, the Weather allows it? box gives the answer for its next run: Yes, or No with the check that holds it back (the rain forecast with its millimetres, the wind...). It is left out when no schedule of the program takes the weather into account.
  • Only some of the checks (skip_conditions, YAML only, or set by an assistant, for instance skip_conditions: [rain_sensor, freeze] on the schedule; see YAML-only options): a list choosing which of the skip conditions this schedule applies, among postponed, rain_sensor, freeze, wind, precipitation, days_between and soil_moisture. Left out, all of them apply, as before. Your own postponement always applies when the weather is taken into account. The schedule judges its chosen conditions at the moment it starts, rather than using the day's shared decision; the holds that follow (days between per zone, a moist soil, rain since the calculation) are the same ones, except that a zone is only held by its days between when that condition is chosen, and by a moist soil only when soil_moisture is chosen. Those holds change the zones' durations for the whole day, so they cannot be undone: if a schedule that applies the moist soil hold ran first, a later schedule of the same day that left soil_moisture out finds those zones already at zero. The other way round works: a schedule that left it out first does not stop a later one from applying it. Switching the schedule's weather off in the panel keeps the list but it no longer applies; switched on again, it applies again.

Good to know: the weather holds work on the zones' calculated durations, which all programs share. On a day a weather-aware start has held a zone back, a program that ignores the weather but waters that zone for its calculated duration finds nothing to water. For a zone that must be watered whatever the weather says, give its step a fixed duration.

A schedule that comes due while its program is already running or waiting starts nothing and counts no watering day; the days between irrigations are only reset for the zones that really start. A program deleted or suspended while it runs stops before its next step. Deleting a program or a schedule also clears what was remembered of its last run, so a new schedule never inherits it.

An occurrence counts as fired as soon as it comes due, whatever happens next: a schedule that is suspended, whose program is already running, or that the weather holds back is not tried again for that occurrence. A scheduled run that is waiting for its turn when Home Assistant restarts is not kept (only a queued manual run is, see below): it is lost until the schedule's next occurrence.

The Smart Irrigation schedules are armed when a setting changes, after a calculation and at a new day, like the start trigger.

The length a "must be done" schedule works back from is the one the Planning chart and the program sensors show, with the adjust_program adjustment in force included. Setting or clearing an adjustment arms the schedules again at once, so the start moves with it.

docs.title: Chaining programs
docs.text:
A schedule can start its program after another program, the way backup jobs are chained: "water the beds 10 minutes after the lawn is done". The second program follows the first whatever its length, which changes every day with the weather, so there is no start time to guess and no gap or overlap to fix by hand.

What it is for:

  • One after the other on the same water: the beds after the lawn on the same well, pump or tank, with a pause in between so the well or the tank fills up again (offset_minutes: 30).
  • Something that only makes sense after a watering: a fertiliser program, a line flush, the pots on the terrace on Saturdays only.
  • Programs with their own rules in one sequence: each one keeps its own steps, days and weather, and a third program can follow the second.

In the schedule, set When to After a program, pick the program in Program, and in Minutes after it ends how long to wait once it has finished (0, right away, up to 720; never before). That moment is when the program stays on starts: the end of a run still to come cannot be aimed at, so hard_deadline does not apply either. In YAML:

name: Beds
steps:
  - zones: [Beds, Hedge]
schedules:
  - type: after
    after_program: Lawn
    offset_minutes: 30
    weekdays: [5]                           # Saturdays only (0 is Monday)

The rules:

  • It starts only when the other program really watered: it went to its end, or was cut by its deadline, and at least one zone got water, whether it was started by its own schedule or with Run now. Not when that one was held back by the weather, suspended, already running, had nothing to water, opened nothing because its deadline had passed, or was stopped (Stop, stop_watering, stop_program, a run that replaced it, or the program deleted, suspended or Smart Irrigation switched off while it ran): whoever stopped the watering did not want the next program either.
  • Then it is a start like any other: its own days are judged on the day it would start (a run that ends at 23:50 with a 20 minute offset is judged on the next day), its own weather is judged when it starts, it takes its turn on its supplies, and it starts nothing when its program is suspended or already running. Its own finish can start a third program in turn.
  • Programs cannot start after each other in a loop (A after B after A, or A after itself): the save is refused, and the program list does not offer the program that would close it. A program another one starts after cannot be deleted (the schedule waits for it, switched on or not): Delete the program is greyed out with the reason, until that schedule is changed. A schedule that still waits for a program that is gone (an old backup) says so and never starts.
  • A start waiting for its offset is recorded and survives a restart: one that came due while Home Assistant was down starts late when it is at most 2 hours late, and is given up beyond. A newer finish of the same program (run again by hand during the wait) replaces it.
  • The planning, the week view and the flow place it right after the planned end of the other program, plus the offset, on the days its filters allow, and only after a run of that program that is expected to water: one the forecast holds back, suspended or with nothing to water starts nothing after it, and nothing is planned when that program is not planned in the window.

docs.title: Irrigate all zones now
docs.text: The Irrigate all zones button of the hub device runs every zone that has a valve once, as a one-off: it is not a program and has no schedule. Its order (one after the other or all at once), its passes and its pause between zones are in Watering > Programs, folded at the bottom of the card under Settings of the Irrigate all zones button, in the advanced mode (the block shows in every mode once one of them is changed: all at once, more than one pass or a pause). They change nothing to the programs, which water their own steps. The run takes its turn on every supply, fires smart_irrigation_irrigation_started and smart_irrigation_irrigation_finished, and credits each zone for what it delivered.

docs.title: Driving the watering
docs.text:
The Programs card: each program's header row has its actions as icons, beside its name and its state (running, paused or waiting for its turn, with the step and the time left): Run now, Stop this program while it is under way, Edit in YAML, and the Options for this run (a total duration, and whether to replace what is running) for the next press of Run now. Pause, Next step and Stop for everything that is watering are on the Home page, while something waters. And these services:

Service What it does smart_irrigation.run_program Runs a program now, or when it is its turn. Optional seconds (1 to 86400) is a total for the whole program, shared between its steps in proportion to their planned durations; left out, the planned durations. A program that is already running or waiting, or suspended, is not run, with a line in the log. A program whose schedules are all off runs all the same: they only decide when it starts on its own. Optional mode: queue (default) takes the turn behind what is running, replace first stops what runs and waits, cleanly (valves closed, delivered water credited), then runs the program. smart_irrigation.water_zone Waters a zone for a number of seconds of water, or for its calculated duration. With mode: queue (default) it takes its turn like everything else; with mode: replace it first stops what is running and waiting. With several zones, only the first replaces, the others follow it. A zone you suspended is watered anyway: asking for it by hand overrides the suspension. smart_irrigation.stop_program Stops one program: if it runs, its open zones close the normal way and are credited for what they delivered, and no further step starts; if it waits for its turn, it is taken out of the queue. An unknown id does nothing. smart_irrigation.set_step_enabled, set_schedule_enabled Switch one of a program's steps (step_id) or one of its schedules (schedule_id) on or off (enabled), as the panel does (set_program_enabled is deprecated): the schedules are armed again and the panel refreshes. With the full controller off nothing changes; an unknown program, step or schedule id is refused with an error. smart_irrigation.pause_watering Closes the open valves and holds everything, the zones waiting included. The clock stops: what was delivered is credited and, after the resume, the part of the pass still owed is watered. A pause that is not lifted ends by itself after an hour (or the minutes given). smart_irrigation.resume_watering Goes on from where the pause stopped. smart_irrigation.next_step Ends the zones of the step a program is on, and lets it go on. With overlapping steps, it ends every step that is open. Programs on supplies of their own water side by side: program_id moves only that one on, and without it every program that is running moves on. smart_irrigation.stop_watering Stops now: every valve is closed, each zone is credited for the water it delivered, programs and waiting zones end. With zones chosen, only those, and the programs under way or waiting do not water those zones in their later steps either. Without zones it also ends a pause. smart_irrigation.suspend Keeps a zone or a program from watering for some hours or until a date. Zero hours lifts it. Hours are limited to 8760, a date that cannot be read is refused (it never lifts a suspension), and an unknown program id is ignored. smart_irrigation.adjust_program Makes a program water longer or shorter for a while (Irrigation Unlimited's adjust_time): a percent (0 to 1000) of every step's water, and/or seconds added to it, for hours (1 to 8760) or until reset. It replaces the previous adjustment instead of adding to it, applies to the runs that start after it is set (not to the one under way), survives a restart, and reset: true clears it. Refused when the full controller is off, and for an unknown program id. The program's sensor shows it in the adjustment attribute. smart_irrigation.use_measured_throughput Takes the flow a zone's meter measured as its throughput. The measurement is advice and is never applied on its own.

docs.title: Seeing what is going on
docs.text:
• The Planning page draws what the programs will water over the next days (3, 7 or 14) as a chart: hover a run for its zones and minutes, why the weather may hold it back, and what it waits for or starts after; a click opens its program. Under it, the Watering now card shows what is watering now: the step, the round, how far along, the valves that are open and for how much longer. Each planned run carries its expected seconds. For a run in the next 48 hours (as far as the rain forecast reaches) it also says when the forecast would hold it back: skipped_reason is precipitation, with the forecast and threshold behind it. A run that ignores the weather, or one further away, gets no reason: the weather is not known days ahead, and a planned run goes ahead if nothing holds it back. Only forecast conditions are predicted, not what the sensors read now. The planning lists the schedules that are on, and ignores suspensions and postponements: a suspended program still appears. For each run, steps lists the zones of the first round only, while expected_seconds covers all the rounds. The data also carries forecast_known (whether a forecast could be read) and sheltered_zone_ids (the zones that still run on a day the rain holds back), but the panel shows only the forecast rain (forecast_mm).
  • A dry zone nothing will water. Once a day, an automatic zone whose water balance has been dry for more than 3 days while no program covers it raises a repair notice (one per zone) and fires smart_irrigation_zone_unwatered. Dry means a deficit of at least half the zone's maximum water balance, or its irrigation threshold when that is larger (never under 1 mm). Covered means a program that is not suspended has an enabled schedule and an enabled step with the zone. A zone you suspended yourself is left alone. The notice clears when the zone is watered or a program covers it again. The count of dry days starts again after a restart or after any reload of the integration. The check also runs at once whenever the programs are changed, so a zone that a new program covers stops being a candidate straight away.
  • One sensor per program (sensor.smart_irrigation_program_<id>): idle, waiting, running, paused or suspended, with the next start, the last run, the suspension and, while it runs, the step and how far along. See entities for the attributes.
  • A check while a valve is open. Every 60 seconds, the zone's linked valve is read. If it reads off, closed or closing, it shut by itself (a water-shortage auto-close, a timed-off that ran out, somebody closing it at the device): smart_irrigation_valve_out_of_sync is fired, with a smart_irrigation_zone_problem of reason valve_closed_early, and the zone's run ends. The valve is not opened again, so a device that closed for lack of water stays shut. The zone is credited for the time the valve was open, taken from the moment its state changed (or, failing that, the moment the check noticed it, so the credit is then exact to about a minute). A valve that reads unknown or unavailable is never taken for a closed one. Only the linked valve is checked, not the extra ones.
  • Events. The other events keep firing too.
  • smart_irrigation_program_started: program_id, program (the name), manual, tours (the rounds), zones (the first round only, each {zone_id, zone, seconds}) and resumed: true when the run goes on after a restart.
  • smart_irrigation_program_finished: program_id, program, manual, zones (what was watered, with seconds, volume_l and the new water balance), problems ({zone_id, zone, reason}) and stopped. A program that starts after this one starts when zones is not empty and stopped is false, or cut is true. A run cut at its deadline adds cut: true and reason: "deadline". It is not fired for a plan with nothing to water, nor for a run taken out of the queue before its turn.
